Intravesical BCG uses a weak bacterium to trigger the immune system to attack cancer cells and is typically started 3 to 6 weeks after TURBT, with maintenance therapy involving three weekly treatments at 3 and 6 months post-TURBT, continued every 6 months for up to 3 years depending on recurrence risk. BCG therapy lowers the chance of cancer coming back or invading bladder muscle and is prioritized for patients at highest risk. Intravesical chemotherapy, given as a one-time dose within 24 hours of TURBT or once weekly for 6 weeks starting 3 to 4 weeks after surgery, kills actively growing cancer cells and only affects the bladder, avoiding severe systemic side effects though it may cause side effects similar to BCG. It is an alternative to BCG when unavailable or ineffective. Both therapies aim to destroy residual cancer cells and prevent new cancer formation.

Clinical trials are medical research studies that assess the safety and effectiveness of investigational treatments, including drugs, devices, and treatment approaches, after they have been developed and tested in a laboratory. These trials study potential new ways of fighting cancer in people and determine whether a treatment is safe and effective before it may be approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). A drug applied to the skin becomes active and kills cancer cells when exposed to light, while devices such as MRI machines detect breast cancer spread to the brain or spine; brain MRI uses a device around the head, while spine MRI does not. Clinical trials provide access to investigational treatments that may eventually be approved by the FDA. Treatment plans are not one-size-fits-all and include multiple options, such as clinical trials, with clear notes on side effects, goals, and chances of a good outcome.

The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck, composed of right and left lobes connected by the isthmus, that produces hormones such as thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which regulate metabolism, body temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, weight, and other body functions. These hormones are essential for proper body function and are transported via the bloodstream. Blood tests measure thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), thyroglobulin (Tg), and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (Tg ab); rising Tg levels may indicate cancer recurrence, while decreasing Tg ab levels may suggest treatment effectiveness. Most thyroid cancers are curable with appropriate treatment, often surgery. Endocrine therapy, also known as hormone therapy, stops hormone production or blocks hormone actions to slow tumor growth or shrink tumors, and may be used in hormone-related cancers like breast cancer. A SSTR-PET/CT scan uses a somatostatin receptor (SSTR) antagonist to detect tumors expressing SSTRs, which are found on many cell types.

Lung cancer is a type of lung carcinoma, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) being the most common form. NSCLC arises from uncontrolled growth of lung cells that do not die when they should, form tumors, and can spread outside the lung. Risk factors include exposure to radon, asbestos, arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium, nickel, coal smoke, soot, silica, diesel fumes, fine particulates, ozone, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide. Smokers are significantly more likely to develop lung cancer and are at higher risk than non-smokers. Lung cancer has stages, unlike acute myeloid leukemia (AML), which does not due to its origin in bone marrow and spread through blood. Regular screening helps detect lung cancer at its earliest, most treatable stages. Neuroendocrine tumors are another type of lung carcinoma, with information available at Airways of the lungs. Cancers that have spread to the lungs are not classified as lung cancer. Chemopreventive agents may help prevent cancer, and patients may consider clinical trials for prevention.

Air moves through the trachea, which splits into two bronchi that lead to the lungs. Each bronchus branches into lobes—right lung has three, left has two—and further divides into bronchioles, ending in alveoli where oxygen is transferred to the blood. The airways include the bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli. Most lung cancers are carcinomas that originate in the cells lining these airways, including the bronchus, bronchioles, and alveoli. The main types are non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which includes adenocarcinoma (most common, from alveolar cells), large cell carcinoma (from large cells in airways), and squamous cell carcinoma (from bronchial cells), and small cell lung cancer. NSCLC is the most common lung carcinoma. Breast cancer can spread to the lungs but remains breast cancer. Lung function tests measure air volume, flow, oxygen use, and carbon dioxide exhalation.

Radical cystectomy is the most widely used surgery for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, involving removal of the entire bladder, nearby lymph nodes, and other organs such as the urethra, prostate, seminal vesicles, uterus, ovaries, fallopian tubes, and part of the vagina or vagina. It requires a hospital stay of at least several days and recovery of 2 to 3 months or longer, with side effects including constipation, diarrhea, bleeding, bowel problems, infections, and changes in sexual function. The procedure is performed under anesthesia, with the urologist inserting an instrument through the urethra into the bladder to examine and remove tumors, a process known as transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT), which also confirms diagnosis, samples the bladder wall, and removes visible tumors. TURBT does not require abdominal incision and is performed in an operating room, clinic, or hospital. A urinary diversion is required and performed simultaneously with radical cystectomy to provide a new pathway for urine to exit the body. Partial cystectomy, rarely used, removes only part of the bladder and is eligible for fewer than 1 in 20 patients with cancer confined to a removable spot. Trimodal therapy—combining TURBT, radiation, and chemotherapy—can serve as a bladder-preserving alternative in some cases.

Chapter 2 covers testing for AML, including genetic and biomarker mutation testing, and discusses fertility impacts of treatment. Chapter 5 addresses treatment of APL, a rare AML subtype, and treatment for BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL, where clinical trials are the preferred option. Chapter 7 provides information on patient advocacy groups and where to get help. Chapter 9 includes a list of suggested questions for patients to ask their care team, encouraging patient involvement in co-creating care plans. Supportive care addresses cancer challenges and enhances life for lung cancer patients, while clinical trials offer hope for various cancers, including lung, pancreatic, and certain leukemias. Radiation therapy and chemoradiation are treatment options for some cancers, with details in specific chapters. Treatment for chondrosarcoma is usually surgery, and for Ewing sarcoma, it begins with systemic therapy. Patients are advised to discuss clinical trials with their care team and to communicate symptoms and needs for optimal care.

External beam radiation therapy (EBRT) is a common form of radiation treatment that uses high-energy x-rays or waves similar to x-rays to destroy small areas of cancer. It is delivered in small daily doses called fractions over a typical course of 5 to 6 weeks, with sessions usually given once daily, Monday through Friday. EBRT uses a linear accelerator to direct radiation at the cancer site, including the chest wall, infraclavicular region, supraclavicular area, or lymph nodes, and is often used in combination with surgery, systemic therapies, or chemotherapy. Lymph node radiation is known as regional nodal irradiation (RNI). Side effects include skin irritation, redness, tenderness, sores, fatigue, diarrhea, nausea, and frequent urination, which often worsen at the end of treatment and take weeks to resolve. Long-term effects may include skin hardening, color changes, spider veins, non-healing ulcers, cataracts, or a second cancer, especially in young patients years later. EBRT is used for various cancers, including cervical, thyroid, and bladder cancer, and is typically administered by a radiation oncologist.

PD-L1 is an immune protein expressed on cancer cells that causes immune cells to ignore the cancer and suppress the anti-tumor immune response. It is measured using a combined positive score (CPS); if CPS is at least 1 percent, treatment options include chemotherapy combined with or alone an immune checkpoint inhibitor. PD-1 is another immune protein that, when expressed on cancer cells, has the same effect. Tumor mutational burden (TMB) is defined as 10 or more mutations per million base pairs of tumor DNA, classified as TMB-H. Metastatic or unresectable TMB-H cancers are treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting PD-1 and PD-L1. These inhibitors activate the immune system to fight cancer cells. Both PD-1 and PD-L1 are key immune checkpoint proteins exploited by tumors to evade immune detection.

The best treatment for cancer is individualized, determined by a medical team that includes experts, scientists, and nurses, and follows best practices grounded in science and expert consensus. These practices, developed at top cancer centers through recent research, guide treatment decisions for advanced-stage prostate and pancreatic cancers. A multidisciplinary team (MDT) of health care and psychosocial professionals with expertise in specific cancers, such as breast cancer, collaborates to plan and implement treatment. While staging is not used for initial pancreatic cancer treatment, experts use a different system to decide therapy, and they are actively studying and developing new treatments. Patients are encouraged to advocate by discussing care options with their care team, choosing an MDT, and reading resources based on current best practices. Treatment options have expanded due to improved detection and therapies, though some cancers remain challenging. The care team unites in treatment planning, with some members involved throughout care and others only during specific phases.

Advanced-stage prostate cancer has spread outside the prostate to nearby areas (regional prostate cancer) or distant parts of the body (metastatic prostate cancer), a process known as metastasis. It is typically a lifelong disease, with treatment aimed at slowing cancer growth, reducing symptoms, and prolonging life. Regional prostate cancer spreads to nearby lymph nodes but not farther, while metastatic prostate cancer spreads to bones, liver, lungs, or other organs. Molecular biomarker testing, using a biopsy sample to analyze molecular components, helps determine the likelihood of cancer spread and is recommended for localized, regional, or metastatic prostate cancer. The book focuses on advanced-stage prostate cancer, which is also referred to as metastatic prostate cancer. Treatment does not cure the disease in most cases but can manage progression and improve quality of life.

Making decisions about cancer care can be stressful for patients and families, involving tough decisions under pressure and complex choices. These decisions are often made under stress and require input from respected experts, with recommendations based on the latest research and practices from leading cancer centers. The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are trusted by both patients and providers and clearly explain current care recommendations. Technologies like blue light cystoscopy and narrow-band imaging may detect tumors more distinctly than white light cystoscopy, but both are still in the testing phase and require further research to determine if they can replace standard methods. Clinical trials are available for primary CNS lymphoma patients, allowing them to receive treatment while contributing to research. Cancer care varies from person to person.

Normal cells follow body rules by increasing only when needed and dying when old or damaged, while leukemia cells do not follow these rules, multiplying quickly, avoiding death, and crowding out normal cells. Leukemia cells often have excess methyl groups in DNA, which block gene activity; hypomethylating agents (HMAs) like azacitidine (Vidaza) and decitabine (Dacogen) block these methyl groups, allowing silenced genes to reactivate and enabling leukemic blasts to mature into normal cells. Chemotherapy, the standard of care for acute myeloid leukemia (AML), kills fast-dividing cells including both cancer and normal cells. It is often administered in a multi-agent regimen, combining two or more drugs, and may be used before or after surgery. Chemotherapy is effective but affects normal cells, leading to side effects. Multiple treatment regimens may be considered standard of care, and patients should consult their care team about options, including clinical trials.

A primary tumor forms over time from cancer cells that behave unlike normal cells and can spread through blood or lymph vessels to distant sites, forming metastases or secondary tumors. Invasive breast cancer spreads from milk ducts or glands into surrounding breast tissue and nearby lymph nodes. The sentinel lymph node is the first lymph node where cancer cells are likely to spread from the primary tumor; a sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) removes these nodes to determine if cancer has spread, and is performed before or during mastectomy or lumpectomy. Inflammatory breast cancer is commonly treated with a modified radical mastectomy, which removes the breast and axillary sentinel lymph nodes. Local therapy, including mastectomy, radiation, and systemic therapy, targets the breast, chest wall, and lymph node area. Breast reconstruction is an option after mastectomy and is typically done in stages, known as delayed reconstruction, after completing cancer treatment.

Pancreatic cancer has a hereditary component in about 1 in 10 cases, with risk passed through genes from parents, particularly in families with close blood relatives who have pancreatic, breast, ovarian, colorectal cancers, or melanoma. Known hereditary conditions that increase risk include Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, familial malignant melanoma syndrome (FAMMM), and hereditary pancreatitis. Genetic tests detect mutations linked to these conditions and are used to assess risk and guide treatment decisions. While surgery is not typically the best treatment due to tumor size, location, or overall health, chemotherapy is often used first to shrink tumors. Drug treatment is commonly used to control cancer growth and reduce symptoms. A multidisciplinary care team, working at a high-volume center experienced in pancreatic cancer, is essential for diagnosis and treatment. Treatment plans may change due to new testing results, side effects, or health conditions.

Cytarabine (Ara-C) is an antimetabolite and an anthracycline used in various treatment regimens; it prevents the use of DNA building blocks and may be given as a single dose to reduce very high white blood cell counts. It has different doses—standard, high (HiDAC), intermediate, and low (LDAC)—with the specific dose determined by many factors and provided by the care team. Cytarabine is included in the dual-drug liposome CPX-351 (Vyxeos), which also contains daunorubicin and includes both an antimetabolite and an anthracycline. Antimetabolites, such as cytarabine, clofarabine, and fludarabine, inhibit DNA synthesis by blocking building blocks of DNA. Anthracyclines, including daunorubicin, idarubicin (Idamycin PFS), and mitoxantrone (Novantrone), damage DNA and cause cell death but can lead to heart issues and have a lifetime dose limit.

Maintenance therapy for ovarian cancer, used after successful initial treatment, reduces cancer return and extends time until progression. It is an option for stages 2–4 and includes PARP inhibitors like olaparib, niraparib, and rucaparib, which work best in BRCA-mutated or HRD-positive cancers. Olaparib and niraparib are recommended for BRCA-mutated cancers, with niraparib used if olaparib is not feasible; niraparib can be given for up to 3 years, rucaparib for up to 2 years. For BRCA-mutated cancers without bevacizumab in chemotherapy, PARP inhibitor alone is recommended. Maintenance therapy may continue until cancer progresses or side effects become severe, after which it is discontinued. It is not well studied in stage 2 ovarian cancer, and safety beyond 2 years post-recurrence is unknown. Patients without a BRCA mutation or without a BRCA test may still receive niraparib or rucaparib if cancer is HRD-positive. Ongoing research evaluates treatment order relative to surgery and compares drug efficacy.

Total thyroidectomy is the primary surgical treatment for papillary thyroid cancer, especially when the tumor has grown beyond the thyroid, spread to lymph nodes, exceeds 4 cm in size, or is a high-risk subtype such as follicular variant, tall-cell, or hobnail. Active surveillance is an option for very-low-risk cases, including small tumors (no larger than a pea) without suspicious lymph nodes or high-risk locations, involving regular ultrasound monitoring. After total thyroidectomy, lifelong levothyroxine replacement is required, and radioactive iodine therapy may be used to eliminate residual cancer cells. Follow-up testing begins when no signs of cancer are detected and helps detect early recurrence. Treatment teams include endocrinologists, surgeons, radiologists, and oncologists. Clips used in breast biopsies mark the site for future imaging and treatment, remain until surgery, and are safe for long-term use, including airport security and MRI.

Lobules are structures in the breast that produce breast milk and resemble tiny clusters of grapes; they are also known as milk glands. Ducts are small tubes that carry milk from the lobules to the nipple, where it exits the breast. Ducts connect the lobules to the nipple and are lined by cells that can develop into cancer. Breast cancer often begins in the ducts or lobules and may spread through lymph or blood to lymph nodes or other parts of the body. Invasive breast cancer grows outside the ducts or lobules into surrounding tissue. The areola, a ring of darker skin on the breast, contains the nipple, the raised tip where milk exits.

Doctors and specialists, including colorectal surgeons and healthcare providers trained in high-resolution anoscopy (HRA), evaluate anal cancer, which is rare and requires expert assessment. They can provide information on cancer stage, grade, and diagnosis through invasive tests like biopsy, which involves removing and testing tissue for cancer and carries risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain. Patients should be clear about their treatment goals and treatment expectations, and maintain a notebook to record discussions. Shared decision-making involves patients and doctors sharing information, discussing options, and agreeing on a treatment plan. Multidisciplinary care includes doctors, specialists, and allied health providers working as a team to support patient outcomes. Factors such as biological and genetic factors contribute to differences in cancer outcomes, particularly among racial groups, and specialists are researching these factors and barriers to care. Residents and fellows are doctors in training to become specialists.

Most people may experience pain or burning when urinating and blood in urine for up to two weeks after a TURBT procedure, with a second procedure sometimes needed 2–6 weeks later to ensure complete tumor removal or deeper biopsy. Anal cancer, rare and often mistaken for hemorrhoids, presents with rectal bleeding (also called bleeding from the anus), anal itching, pain, or a lump near the anus, and most people first contact a primary care physician, gynecologist, or gastroenterologist. A gynecologist diagnoses and treats female reproductive organ diseases and may be part of a treatment team for cervical cancer. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) causes infectious mononucleosis and is linked to EBV-related cancer, most notably nasopharyngeal cancer. A neck dissection, involving removal of a gland under general anesthesia, is performed to remove lymph nodes near the thyroid or to address cancer spread, with most people staying overnight and following at-home care. If cancer cells are found in surrounding tissue removed with the tumor, additional treatment is required.

Individuals undergoing cancer treatment are advised to undergo a pregnancy test before starting treatment if they can become pregnant, as cancer and its treatments can harm a developing fetus. Fertility may be temporarily or permanently impaired, with the extent of loss related to age at diagnosis, treatment type, dose, and duration. Preventing pregnancy during and after treatment is essential because cancer and its treatments can affect ovaries and damage sperm. Hormonal birth control may not be recommended for all individuals, so patients should consult their doctor about alternative non-hormonal options such as barrier methods, which include condoms, diaphragms, cervical caps, and the contraceptive sponge. These barrier methods are preferred after a breast cancer diagnosis. Patients should discuss fertility concerns and pregnancy plans with their care team, especially if they plan to have children in the future. Menstruation may stop during treatment but often returns within two years for individuals under 35. If a patient is pregnant or breastfeeding at diagnosis, certain treatments must be avoided.

Patients should inquire about their type of bone cancer, its prognosis, and treatment options, and whether a nearby sarcoma cancer center specializes in it. They should ask about tests, their frequency, insurance coverage, and financial assistance programs, including where to find help for test costs. Healthcare providers will discuss next steps, timing, and prognosis, and may perform a clinical breast exam to check for lumps, nipple discharge, bleeding, skin changes, or enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, underarm, or groin. Standard cancer care is typically billed to and covered by insurance, with patients responsible for copays and uncovered costs, especially during clinical trials where standard care continues. Patients can choose when and on which days to begin treatment, and should prepare by knowing what to avoid or take with caution, bringing a companion, and considering work or school absences. Enrolling in a clinical trial is an option, and patients should seek expert opinion from specialists in their specific cancer type.

Vaginal stenosis, often caused by radiation therapy to the pelvis or surgery, results in a vagina that is narrower, shorter, thinner, drier, and may contain scar tissue, leading to pain during sex and pelvic exams. This condition is a common sexual side effect in anal cancer patients, alongside reduced sex drive, vaginal dryness, and difficulty achieving erections. The Anal Cancer Foundation operates a Peer-To-Peer Support Program that matches patients and caregivers with trained volunteers to provide empathetic connection and practical advice during diagnosis, treatment, and recovery. Sexual health therapists specialize in helping cancer survivors manage these side effects. Organizations such as the American Cancer Society, CancerCare, and Cancer Support Community provide information and support for anal cancer patients. Survivors require ongoing care, including surveillance testing, survivorship care (covered in Chapter 5 and Chapter 7), and additional support for sexual health and overall well-being.

Perineural invasion occurs when a tumor grows into a nerve or group of nerves, indicating high-risk or very high-risk cancer and is associated with symptoms like burning, pain, stinging, loss of feeling, movement, and double or blurred vision. Photodynamic therapy involves applying a light-sensitive drug to the skin, which becomes active under red or blue light to kill cancer cells, and causes side effects including burning, redness, itching, and pain. Topical therapies for skin cancer cause burning, redness, itching, and pain in the treated area and may require re-treatment over time, especially for sun-damaged skin. Radiation therapy causes skin redness, itching, mild discomfort, and fatigue, and cannot be reused on previously treated areas; palliative radiation may be used to relieve symptoms and limit tumor size. Strange skin changes, such as redness, swollen nipple area, or warmth, require immediate medical attention. Metastatic bladder cancer is not curable but is treatable, with improving treatments over time.

Bile, a yellow or green fluid produced by liver cells, contains cholesterol, bilirubin, salts, water, and body elements. It flows from the liver through small channels into ducts, which form the left and right hepatic ducts; these join to create the common hepatic duct. The common hepatic duct joins the cystic duct, which connects to the gallbladder, forming the common bile duct. Bile is stored in the gallbladder and released into the small intestine upon eating to aid fat digestion. The liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts constitute the hepatobiliary system, which also filters blood, aids in blood clotting, and produces factors for body function. Primary liver cancer begins in the liver, with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) being the most common type and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (a bile duct cancer) the second most common. A rare mixed-type tumor combines HCC and cholangiocarcinoma. Secondary liver cancer results when other cancers, such as colon cancer, spread to the liver. The common bile duct also joins the pancreatic duct before entering the small intestine.

T1 tumors, which have not grown beyond the second muscle layer of the rectal wall, are treated with endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), a minimally invasive procedure that removes small rectal cancers in one piece. ESD is performed using an endoscope and a tool that injects fluid to lift and separate the tumor. After treatment, surveillance begins as early as 3 months post-ESD, with imaging (via endorectal ultrasound or pelvic MRI with contrast) and proctoscopies recommended every 3 to 6 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months for the next 3 years, and annually after 5 years. Endorectal ultrasound is an alternative to pelvic MRI, used when a patient has a pacemaker, MRI images are unhelpful, or cancer has not grown far into the rectal wall. Digital rectal exams are recommended every 3 to 6 months for 5 years post-treatment. Blood tests and imaging may be ordered if symptoms or relapse are suspected, and the original CA-125 level may be monitored regularly.

Fatigue is a common and multifaceted symptom in people with cancer, including anal cancer, and can be physical, cognitive, or emotional, often resulting from medication, poor nutrition, or lack of exercise. It is particularly debilitating in glioma patients and not solely related to sleep or activity. Survivorship care resources, such as those available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines, address fatigue, anxiety, depression, distress, cognitive dysfunction, pain, sexual dysfunction, sleep disorders, healthy lifestyles, immunizations, employment concerns, and complementary and alternative therapies. Examples of complementary and alternative therapies include acupuncture, dietary supplements, eastern medicine, medical marijuana, herbal teas, homeopathy, hypnosis, meditation, reiki, yoga, and massage therapy. These therapies may help manage side effects and improve well-being. Support for people with cancer includes cancer navigators, social workers, support groups, talk therapy, exercising, spending time with loved ones, and medication. Pharmacists, especially those specializing in cancer care, assist with medication preparation, use, and side effect discussion. Integrative oncology combines conventional treatments with complementary therapies. Patients are encouraged to consult their treatment team before using any complementary therapy.

Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is an enzyme found in most cells, released into the blood during cell death or in fast-growing tumor cells; high LDH levels may indicate cell damage from cancer or other conditions. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a protein in blood, elevated in colorectal cancer and sometimes in less common ovarian cancers (LCOCs), and monitoring it may help track cancer spread, though it is not useful for everyone. LCOCs are associated with elevated levels of CEA, LDH, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, alpha-fetoprotein, inhibin, CA 19-9, and HE4. Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is a protein on most cells, unique to each person, marking self cells and playing a key role in immune response; HLA typing is a blood test performed before allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant to find a donor match with a very good protein match, as poor matches can lead to rejection. Each person has the same HLA set in all their cells.

PSA is a protein produced by prostate cells, primarily found in semen and in small amounts in the bloodstream. An unusually high PSA level may indicate prostate cancer, but it does not confirm it, as age, an enlarged prostate, or urinary tract infection can also cause elevated levels. The PSA test alone cannot diagnose prostate cancer and is typically paired with a digital rectal exam or imaging to assess risk and determine if a biopsy is needed. If cancer cells are found in a biopsy, further testing evaluates the cancer's growth rate—whether it grows quickly or slowly—helping to plan treatment. Biomarker tests, such as additional blood or urine tests, may be used alongside PSA to decide if further testing is necessary. Prostate cancer results from uncontrolled growth of prostate cells, and researchers do not know its exact cause. A biopsy is the only definitive way to confirm prostate cancer.

Intravesical therapy is a treatment for bladder cancer that involves filling the bladder with liquid medication to destroy cancer cells, typically delivered via a catheter inserted into the urethra through a process called instillation. It is used to target residual or hard-to-reach cancer cells after procedures like TURBT and to prevent new cancer formation. The therapy may cause side effects such as frequent urination, bladder inflammation, pain, or blood in urine. A catheter, a thin tube inserted into a large vein in the upper arm or chest, or a port—a small, round disc placed under the skin in the upper chest—may be used to deliver chemotherapy drugs like 5-FU, which is given by continuous infusion over several days. These devices are tailored to individual needs and remain in place until treatment ends. Symptoms of bladder cancer include frequent urination, urgency, painful urination, and back pain, prompting individuals to seek medical evaluation for diagnosis.

A biomarker is a sign of disease, abnormality, or condition, and in cancer care, testing looks for changes in genes, proteins, or markers. Symptoms, defined as problems or feelings that may indicate disease, often signal the presence of conditions like glioma, which is typically detected when it causes pressure on the brain or invades brain tissue. Bladder cancer is usually found when a person has symptoms, most commonly hematuria. Primary CNS lymphoma is also diagnosed when symptoms appear. Gliomas are described by cell type, biomarker (e.g., IDH-mutant), and growth rate (e.g., grade 2). Contrast dye, injected into a vein, enhances tissue and organ visibility in CT and MRI scans and is preferred unless contraindicated by allergy or condition. X-rays use low-dose radiation to detect bone issues and tumors, which show up due to altered radiation absorption. The immune system, including lymphocytes and the lymphatic system, defends against infection and disease, and an impaired immune system increases the risk of primary CNS lymphoma.

Leukemia can spread to the spinal fluid (CSF) surrounding the spine and brain, causing headaches, neck pain, and sensitivity to light. Imaging tests may detect leukemia in lymph nodes, liver, spleen, skin, or bone, but rarely in the brain and spinal cord lining. Leukemia is associated with coagulopathy, an impaired clotting process common in the disease, which may result in bleeding, bruising, or blood clots due to defective coagulation factors produced by the liver. A lumbar puncture may be performed to check for leukemia cells in the spinal fluid. If cancer cells are found in the cerebrospinal fluid or an MRI shows spinal involvement, intrathecal or intra-CSF chemotherapy may be administered. Breast cancer can metastasize to the spine, but leukemia does not commonly spread to the brain or spinal cord lining. The spine consists of 24 vertebrae (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar), including the sacrum and coccyx.

BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene mutations increase the risk of breast, ovarian, prostate, colorectal, pancreatic, and melanoma (skin) cancers. These inherited (germline) mutations can be passed from parents to children and carried by siblings. Germline testing, which examines BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, and PMS2 genes, is recommended for individuals with prostate cancer, family histories of breast, ovarian, intestinal, or other cancers, high-risk or metastatic prostate cancer, or Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry. Mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2 are specifically linked to melanoma and colorectal cancer via MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2. Germline testing uses blood, urine, or saliva and helps determine inherited cancer risk, interpret results, and guide treatment decisions, including eligibility for targeted therapies like PARP inhibitors. Having a mutation increases cancer risk but does not guarantee cancer development. Melanoma is a less common but more aggressive form of skin cancer. Genetic counselors, trained in genetic diseases, assist in deciding whether to undergo testing and interpreting results.

The prostate is a gland located in the lower body, about the size of a ping-pong ball, and is part of the male reproductive system. It produces semen by making a fluid component and secreting prostate-specific antigen, which nourishes and helps transmit semen; it also contains muscles that propel semen through the urethra during ejaculation. The seminal vesicles, located above and behind the prostate, produce and store a fluid component of semen. Semen is a fluid composed of prostate and seminal vesicle fluids, plus sperm from the testicles, and is released during ejaculation through the urethra and exits via the penis. The male reproductive system includes the penis, seminal vesicles, testicles, and prostate. Having a close family member, such as a sibling or parent, with prostate cancer increases an individual's risk, and an inherited mutation in the BRCA2 gene also raises this risk. Cancer occurs when cell growth goes wrong and can spread outside the prostate to other parts of the body.

Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) is a rare, aggressive form of breast cancer that occurs more frequently in persons assigned female at birth, though it can also affect individuals assigned male at birth. IBC arises when cancer cells block lymph vessels in the skin of the breast, causing redness, swelling, warmth, and a peau d’orange appearance, often mimicking infection. It is typically diagnosed via biopsy of affected skin and is mostly a type of invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC), which begins in milk duct cells and spreads into surrounding tissue. IBC lacks a palpable lump and is difficult to diagnose early. Treatment includes chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radiation therapy, mastectomy, endocrine therapy, HER2-targeted therapy, supportive care, and clinical trials, with side effects discussed. While treatment options are similar across genders, IBC is distinct due to its rapid progression and unique presentation.

A karyotype is a picture of chromosomes, showing extra, missing, rearranged, or abnormal pieces, and requires growing cells obtained from a blood sample or bone marrow. Normal human cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes, totaling 46. A complex karyotype involves three or more unrelated changes or deletions in multiple cells. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) uses probes that attach to specific DNA sequences to detect known changes, including missing parts and extra copies of chromosomes, such as 17p deletion, and can be performed on blood or bone marrow without needing growing cells. AML mutation testing uses karyotype, FISH, NGS, and PCR to detect abnormalities unique to AML cells, including gene and chromosome mutations. DNA controls cell growth and function and is tightly packaged into chromosomes; UV radiation can harm DNA, leading to conditions like basal cell skin cancer. The care team uses this information to plan treatment.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a slow-worsening cancer of lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, characterized by abnormal B cells that grow out of control and crowd out healthy B cells, impairing their function and leading to fewer healthy blood cells and a higher risk of infection. CLL may be detected during routine blood testing and often presents no symptoms initially; when symptoms occur, they include swollen glands, fatigue, night sweats, fever, recurrent infections, loss of appetite, and unintentional weight loss. Treatment is individualized and may not be needed immediately but can be required if white blood cell counts rise rapidly, normal blood cells are low, lymph nodes are enlarged, or symptoms appear. Treatment options include daily pills or combinations of IV infusions and pills, and should be discussed with a doctor. There is no cure for CLL, but effective treatment helps maintain healthy blood cells and enables a full life. The goal of treatment is to prevent CLL from causing problems or becoming life-threatening. CLL cells commonly express CD20, CD200, and LEF1, distinguishing them from mantle cell lymphoma, which lacks CD200 and LEF1. Richter transformation, a rare complication, can lead to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or Hodgkin lymphoma.

Surveillance for nonmetastatic anal canal cancer (stages I–III) involves regular follow-up visits and physical exams. A follow-up exam with digital rectal examination (DRE) and anoscopy is recommended 8 to 12 weeks after completing chemoradiation to assess treatment results. DRE and lymph node exams are performed every 3 to 6 months for 5 years, while anoscopy is recommended every 6 to 12 months for 3 years. Visit frequency adjusts based on individual risk of recurrence and patient or provider preference, with higher-risk individuals needing more frequent exams. After year 5, visits are typically once a year or on an agreed schedule. Radiation therapy may cause discomfort or pain, preventing anoscopy in some patients, in which case the patient and doctor may decide to omit it or perform it less often. Surveillance is the same for anal canal and perianal cancer. Nonmetastatic means the cancer has not spread beyond the pelvis or to distant sites. Imaging is recommended annually for 3 years after recurrence treatment.

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), also known as SCC, is the most common type of cervical cancer, nasopharyngeal cancer, mouth cancer, and throat cancer, and is more prevalent in Eastern Europe, Asia, and Africa. It arises in squamous cells lining the ectocervix and can form in damaged, inflamed, or scarred skin, where it is difficult to treat and more likely to recur. Adenocarcinoma, arising in glandular cells of the endocervical canal, is the second most common cervical cancer type. Adenosquamous carcinoma, a rare mixed tumor containing both squamous and glandular elements, is less common than SCC. Most esophageal cancers are adenocarcinomas in North America and Western Europe, while SCC dominates in Eastern Europe, Asia, and Africa. Recommended treatment options for SCC, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma are presented in Part, with neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix being the rarest and most aggressive cervical cancer type, treated separately.

Adrenal cancer, also known as adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC), is a rare cancer originating in the adrenal glands, most commonly affecting children aged 5 and under and adults in their 40s and 50s. ACC is the most common type of adrenal gland cancer and begins in the adrenal cortex; it can be functioning or nonfunctioning, with functioning tumors potentially producing multiple hormones. Half of individuals with adrenal cancer experience symptoms due to hormone overproduction, while others develop symptoms from tumor growth pressing on nearby organs. Common symptoms include back pain, unexplained weight loss, hormonal changes (such as excess facial hair, hair loss, irregular periods, enlarged breast tissue, or shrinking testicles), nausea, vomiting, abdominal bloating, and loss of appetite. Symptoms may also include pain in the pelvis or belly, frequent urination, and feeling bloated. If the cancer spreads beyond the adrenal glands, cure becomes less likely. Treatment can delay progression or recurrence, and early detection improves the likelihood of cure. Most adrenal tumors have no known cause, though hereditary conditions increase risk.

Esophageal and stomach cancers originate in the innermost lining (mucosa) of these organs. Esophageal cancer includes squamous cell carcinoma, which arises in flat squamous cells of the upper and middle esophagus, and adenocarcinoma, which begins in mucus-producing cells of the lower esophagus. Stomach cancer primarily involves adenocarcinomas that start in mucus-secreting cells of the stomach lining and are classified as intestinal (cells forming tube- or gland-like structures, more treatable with targeted therapy) or diffuse (cells scattered, less common). Both cancers grow through the organ wall and spread to nearby lymph nodes, veins, arteries, and organs such as the liver, pancreas, spleen, and lung. The presence of tumor invasion into blood vessels or arteries may indicate unresectable disease, making surgical removal unsafe. Mucus is secreted in the submucosa of the esophagus and stomach, and both cancers can form ulcers or masses that cause symptoms.

Head and neck cancer can affect the jaw, teeth, and gums, and patients should inform their dentist and maintain regular dental cleanings and checkups. Dental work may be recommended before starting cancer treatment to address potential issues. A panoramic dental x-ray, also known as a Panorex, uses a very small dose of radiation to capture the entire mouth, including teeth, upper and lower jaws, and surrounding structures and tissues, and is commonly performed by dentists and oral surgeons. It may be used to plan treatment for dentures, braces, extractions, and implants. Nonkeratinized squamous epithelium covers the soft palate, inner lips, inner cheeks, floor of the mouth, and area underneath the tongue, while keratinized squamous epithelium is found on the gums, hard palate, and top of the tongue. HPV testing is recommended for all patients diagnosed with oropharyngeal cancer.

A genetic counselor is specially trained to help individuals understand genetic diseases and decide whether to undergo germline testing, which aims to detect inherited mutations present in every cell of the body. Germline testing is recommended for individuals who have had cancer, have a close relative with bladder cancer, are under 50, have upper urinary tract or high-grade cancer, or have Lynch syndrome or a family member with it. These mutations can be passed to children and are distinct from somatic mutations, which occur only in tumor cells. Testing uses blood, saliva, or urine samples and may take days or weeks; results can guide treatment planning and are discussed with a genetic counselor. A strong family history of cancer or a positive test result may prompt consultation with a genetic counselor. Quitting smoking improves cancer treatment outcomes, reduces cancer and disease risk, and enhances bladder cancer treatment effectiveness, though it is difficult and help is available to improve success.

The pancreas is a deep organ located below the liver and behind the stomach, about 6 inches long, that produces digestive enzymes to break down proteins, fats, sugars, and starches, and hormones like insulin and glucagon to regulate blood sugar. It is part of the digestive system and functions closely with the liver, gallbladder, stomach, spleen, and small intestine. Pancreatic adenocarcinomas, also known as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), are the most common type of pancreatic cancer and arise from exocrine cells lining the pancreas ducts. These cancers disrupt normal cell growth by causing cells to multiply uncontrollably, fail to die when they should, and form tumors that may spread to nearby tissues and distant areas. The pylorus connects the stomach to the duodenum and regulates the passage of food during digestion.

An MRI machine is a large device with a tunnel in the middle, similar to a CT scanner but without radiation. It uses powerful magnets and radio waves to produce images of the inside of the body. Patients lie on a table that slides into the tunnel and must remain still to obtain clear images; straps or padded head braces may be used to prevent movement. The scan may cause the body to feel warm and produces loud noises, which can be reduced with earplugs or music. MRI is used to evaluate the liver, rectum, lymph nodes, and bones in the pelvis, and may be ordered when CT results are unclear or to better visualize cancer near the rectum, where a gel or enema may be inserted beforehand. For small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix, an MRI of the brain is recommended. MRI is the most useful imaging technique for identifying primary CNS lymphoma. Patients should inform their doctor if they have had contrast problems or are sensitive to tight spaces.

Primary CNS lymphoma and other brain tumors can cause problems with brain function, including slower thinking, memory loss, difficulty moving or walking, trouble speaking, changes in behavior, and loss of sense of self. These symptoms may be similar to those of other neurological illnesses or brain cancers, so diagnosis requires imaging and removal of tumor tissue for testing. Whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT) is used to treat primary CNS lymphoma, especially when tumors are widespread, and it can reach the brain, spine, and eyeballs, though it carries risks of long-term cognitive issues and damage to fine motor skills like handwriting and tying shoes. Radiation therapy was historically the main treatment, especially before chemotherapy, and remains an option for those who cannot receive chemotherapy during the induction phase. Helping a person with a brain tumor is challenging and time-consuming, involving physical, mental, emotional, and hands-on support, such as attending appointments, reducing side effects, and assisting with treatment decisions. Support should be gathered early, including from online resources.

A cancer diagnosis can trigger strong, fluctuating feelings such as sadness, fear, helplessness, worry, anger, guilt, depression, anxiety, and sleep issues, which are collectively referred to as distress. Distress is an unpleasant mental, physical, social, or spiritual experience that affects how a person feels, thinks, and acts. It may vary from day to day or week to week. Patients are encouraged to talk to their care team or trusted individuals about their emotional state. Support and counseling services are available, and many treatment teams include mind and body therapists who can assist with emotional and physical well-being. Treatment teams routinely screen patients’ levels of distress as part of cancer care. Distress can also impact family or loved ones, who may experience anxiety or depression and can seek help from a social worker.

Bright spots on PET scans can result from cancer cells, normal organs like the brain, heart, kidneys, and bladder, or inflammation and infection. Inflammation and infection can both appear as bright spots and are linked to immune stressors such as infections or inflammatory responses. In lymph nodes, temporary germinal centers form in response to infection or inflammation, and unregulated growth of lymphocytes within these centers can lead to follicular lymphoma (FL). Radiation therapy for primary CNS lymphoma in the eyes may cause vision problems and cataracts, which can be treated with a routine operation by an eye surgeon. Intraocular chemotherapy may cause infection, inflammation, and cataracts. Cataracts can also develop as a side effect of radiation therapy and are treatable via operation. Lymphocytes, which fight and prevent infection, normally grow in response to infection or inflammation but can develop into lymphoma if growth is unregulated.

The female reproductive system includes the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina, functioning together for sexual reproduction. A hysterectomy removes the uterus and cervix, and when the cervix is removed, it is called a total hysterectomy; it results in no possibility of pregnancy and may remove ovaries, causing surgical premature menopause. A bilateral salpingooophorectomy removes both ovaries and fallopian tubes. Pelvic exenteration removes all remaining reproductive organs. Radiation therapy can cause premature ovarian insufficiency or radiation-induced premature menopause. An applicator is inserted into the uterus through the vagina and connected to a brachytherapy machine; a radiation source travels through hollow tubes into the applicator, used when a hysterectomy is not performed, preserving the option for natural pregnancy. Bilateral oophorectomy is surgery to remove both ovaries.

Blood cells originate from blood stem cells in the red marrow, located in the center of most of the body’s 206 bones, where they mature into red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets. Red marrow, which contains blood stem cells, is often replaced by yellow marrow (mostly fat) as people age. Blood cells are continuously replaced, with red blood cells produced at one million per second and some white blood cells living less than one day. Stem cell rescue involves removing healthy stem cells from the patient’s blood or bone marrow, freezing them, and returning them after chemotherapy damages bone marrow. These stem cells migrate to bone marrow, where they grow into new blood stem cells, restoring infection protection and enabling blood cell regrowth within weeks, with full recovery taking up to a year. The procedure is intense, not suitable for primary CNS lymphoma, and used only after other treatments fail or in case of relapse. Treatment teams evaluate multiple factors to determine suitability.

Levothyroxine prevents thyroid cancer cell growth and is a key part of therapy for differentiated thyroid cancers, taken as a pill on an empty stomach at least 30 minutes before eating to ensure absorption. An optimal dose is determined through trial and error, with non-optimal dosing causing anxiety, sleep disturbances, racing heart, and abnormal heartbeat; excess can lead to weakened bones, heart rhythm issues, and thyrotoxicosis. Providers may recommend calcium and vitamin D supplements to support bone health. Radioactive iodine (iodine-131) therapy targets thyroid cancer cells that absorb iodine, with whole-body radioiodine scans performed before or after treatment to detect residual thyroid tissue or hidden cancer. Providers assess tumor size, subtype, spread, thyroglobulin levels, and age to determine if RAI is appropriate. Targeted therapies, such as kinase inhibitors, are used for advanced or recurrent thyroid cancer. Thyroid nodules are usually non-cancerous and asymptomatic; providers may detect large nodules during physical exams. Providers also evaluate symptoms like bloating, pelvic pain, or difficulty eating, which may indicate ovarian cancer or other conditions.

Prognostic stage incorporates anatomic TNM classification, tumor grade, and biomarkers such as HER2, estrogen receptor (ER), and progesterone receptor (PR), and assumes standard-of-care treatment. It is divided into clinical and pathologic stages. Clinical stage (c) is assigned before any treatment and is based on physical exam, biopsy, and imaging tests, represented by terms like cN2 or cM. Pathologic stage (p) applies to patients who have undergone surgery and is determined by examining surgically removed tissue, represented by terms like pNI or pTNM. Staging is typically performed twice—before and after surgery—with post-surgical staging providing more accurate details about tumor size and lymph node status. Final staging combines available information, and if drug therapy is given before surgery, the stage may be denoted as ypT. Staging helps predict cancer prognosis, which refers to the likely course of the disease, and is essential for treatment decisions.

The ovary is a pair of grape-sized organs in the pelvis, part of the female reproductive system, that produce eggs for sexual reproduction and hormones affecting breast growth, body shape, and the menstrual cycle. Each ovary is located on the left or right side of the uterus and is surrounded by a fallopian tube, which transports eggs to the uterus. If an egg is not fertilized, a period occurs. The uterus requires at least one ovary and one fallopian tube for menstruation and pregnancy. Ovarian transposition, medically known as oophoropexy, is a surgery that relocates one or both ovaries out of the radiation beam's range and may be an option for premenopausal patients with squamous cell carcinoma, the most common type of cervical cancer. Hysterectomy, which removes the uterus, both ovaries, and fallopian tubes, is the most common surgery for ovarian cancer and is also used in early-stage cervical cancer treatment. Fertility-sparing surgery may be an option for early ovarian cancer that has not spread beyond the ovary. Stage 3A1 ovarian cancer involves cancer in the ovaries and spread to retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Most ovarian cancers affect the epithelium, the outer layer of the ovary.

Chondrosarcoma is a type of bone cancer, alongside osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma, and is covered in the NCCN Guidelines for Patients®: Soft Tissue Sarcoma. Ivosidenib is indicated for individuals with chondrosarcoma prone to IDH1 mutations. Multiple myeloma is not a type of bone cancer and is addressed in the NCCN Guidelines for Patients®: Multiple Myeloma. The NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app and NCCN.org/patientguidelines host these guidelines, including those on colorectal cancer screening, immunotherapy side effects (specifically immune checkpoint inhibitors), fertility preservation, colon cancer treatment, early-stage prostate cancer, metastatic breast cancer, and gallbladder and bile duct tumors. All patient resources are available both online and via the app.

Cisplatin and carboplatin are platinum-based chemotherapy drugs that contain platinum and are used to treat ovarian cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, and other cancers. Cisplatin is generally preferred in platinum-based therapy but may cause hearing loss, tinnitus, kidney damage, and peripheral neuropathy, especially in hands and feet, and increases the risk of life-threatening hypersensitivity reactions. Carboplatin is used as an alternative when cisplatin is too harsh or not feasible. These drugs are often combined with taxanes—paclitaxel or docetaxel—forming a common regimen for newly diagnosed stage 1 cancers, with paclitaxel and carboplatin given every 3 weeks. In recurrent or metastatic cancer, cisplatin may be less effective after prior use and is often combined with other medicines. Chemotherapy is administered in cycles with rest days, and patients should consult their treatment team for side effect lists. Platinum-based therapy is effective against cancer and is typically recommended for recurrent platinum-sensitive disease.

Lymph nodes are bean-shaped, fist-sized structures about 4 inches long that filter lymph, catch foreign particles, harmful cells, and cancer cells, and play key roles in blood filtration and storage. They are most numerous in the neck, groin, and armpits and drain lymph from the breast and nearby areas. Abnormal lymph nodes seen on imaging may contain cancer cells and require biopsy. Biopsies such as fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), and core needle biopsy (CNB) use needles to remove tissue or lymph node samples for analysis. FNA and CNB are commonly used to sample tumors or lymph nodes, with FNA also known as needle biopsy. These procedures are guided by imaging in some cases. FNA can suggest but not diagnose follicular thyroid carcinoma or oncocytic carcinoma, which are more likely to spread to lymph nodes and invade blood vessels. Pathologists compile results into formal reports.

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common type of kidney cancer, accounting for 9 out of 10 cases and originating in cells lining the renal tubules. It is categorized into subtypes based on histology, including clear cell RCC (occurring in 7 out of 10 cases) and non-clear cell RCC (nccRCC), with papillary RCC being the most common nccRCC subtype affecting 1 out of 10 RCC patients. Histology, studied under a microscope, guides treatment decisions and is key in determining treatment plans. RCC may present as multiple tumors in one or both kidneys, which are not considered metastasis but are treated as separate primary tumors. Tumors can grow into the renal vein or vena cava and may develop sarcomatoid features or become sarcomatoid RCC. Kidney cancer can spread to lungs, lymph nodes, bones, and less frequently to liver and brain. When it grows beyond Gerota’s fascia, it indicates advanced disease. A pathology report includes histology information, and an open biopsy may be recommended to confirm histology. Patients should discuss treatment options with their healthcare provider and ask about their specific cancer subtype.

Saliva and blood are used in genetic cancer risk testing to detect germline mutations inherited from birth parents, some of which increase the risk of multiple cancers and can be passed to children. Blood relatives may carry these mutations and are tested for leukemia predisposition syndrome, especially if they are potential hematopoietic cell donors. Biochemical tests measure hormones in blood, urine, or saliva to assess adrenal tumors or tumor-related syndromes. When acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells disappear, remission is achieved, meaning no symptoms or signs of cancer, and can last months or years; during remission, saliva and blood can be used to detect leukemia predisposition syndrome. Testing of cells not affected by leukemia, such as skin cells, also helps identify the syndrome. Patients should inform their care team of a family history of cancer.

A biopsy is the only definitive method to confirm cancer, involving the removal of a tissue sample for laboratory analysis. For primary CNS lymphoma, stereotactic biopsy is the standard method, used when the tumor is in a hard-to-reach or vital area, and removes only enough tissue for diagnosis. Imaging tests, such as MRI, identify potential tumors, and a tissue sample is sent to a pathologist or neuropathologist for microscopic examination to determine cancer type, grade, and biomarkers. Core needle biopsy, performed under light sedation by an interventional radiologist or surgeon, removes a tissue sample without removing the entire lymph node and is commonly used for Hodgkin lymphoma or bone cancer. Surgical biopsy involves a small incision, requires an operating room visit, and is performed by the treating surgeon. A diagnosis of bone cancer is confirmed through core needle or surgical biopsy, with biopsy placement being critical. The testing process takes about one week.

Stem cell rescue, also known as hematopoietic stem cell transplant, uses a patient’s own blood-forming stem cells to restore bone marrow function after high-dose chemotherapy, which destroys both lymphoma cells and stem cells in the bone marrow. The process involves harvesting, freezing, and returning stem cells to regenerate healthy blood cells. It is considered risky for older or frail individuals due to chemotherapy side effects, including low blood counts, infection vulnerability, and fatigue. For patients with primary CNS lymphoma, a thorough eye exam by an eye doctor is required to detect vitreoretinal lymphoma, where lymphoma cells may form in the retina or invade the vitreous. An eye exam using a slit lamp with pupil-dilating drops examines the retina, optic nerve, and other eye structures; if abnormalities or visual symptoms are present, a vitrectomy may be performed to remove and test the vitreous for cancer cells, which can confirm the diagnosis. Treatment begins with an induction phase involving multiple hospital-based chemotherapy courses to eliminate lymphoma cells.

Basal cell skin cancer (BCC), the most common type of skin cancer, arises in basal cells of the epidermis and commonly develops in sun-exposed areas such as the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. It is usually curable because it rarely metastasizes. Tumors on the head, face, neck, hands, feet, shins, or genital areas are considered high risk due to location, and any tumor over 4 cm in size is very high risk due to size. A well-defined tumor border indicates low risk, while an uneven, poorly defined border indicates high risk. BCC is associated with UV light exposure, fair skin, red or blond hair, light eye color, age, and a history of skin cancer. Treatment often involves surgery, with PDEMA/Mohs surgery being preferred for high-risk sites like the face and head due to its ability to remove cancer while sparing normal tissue. All treatments carry a risk of recurrence.

Actinic keratoses are pre-cancerous, scaly or rough skin lesions caused by long-term sun exposure, appearing as red, white, tan, or pink spots or raised bumps and resembling warts. They may develop into squamous cell skin cancer and increase the risk of it. Treatments include topical therapies such as tirbanibulin (Klisyri), a microtubule inhibitor that kills fast-growing cells and is applied once daily for five consecutive days to the face or scalp using a single-dose packet; 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod (Aldara), which are prescription creams used for both actinic keratoses and early cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC); topical keratolytics like urea, lactic acid, or salicylic acid; photodynamic therapy, cryotherapy, and curettage, which involves scraping skin with a spoon-shaped tool. Superficial treatments affect only the top skin layer and are used for actinic keratoses and Bowen’s disease, which are in the same general area. Early CSCC on the skin surface not spreading to lymph nodes is treated with C&E. All actinic keratoses require medical evaluation by a doctor or dermatologist.

Cervical cancer begins with abnormal microscopic cells on the cervix, known as cervical dysplasia or cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), which may progress to cancer if left untreated. High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL), corresponding to CIN 2 or 3, is considered pre-cancer. Abnormal cells may invade the cervical stroma, leading to cancer. Diagnosis involves a cone biopsy, with margins examined by a pathologist for cancer or pre-cancer. If pre-cancer is found at margins, either an extrafascial hysterectomy or modified radical hysterectomy is recommended, with pelvic lymph node removal in both cases. Treatment depends on stage and risk factors, including lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI), which indicates tumor cells in blood or lymph vessels and increases the risk of lymph node spread. For stage 1A1 cancers with LVSI, modified radical hysterectomy with lymph node evaluation is recommended; for stage 1A2 and 1B1, extrafascial hysterectomy with lymph node evaluation is advised if low-risk. Radical trachelectomy is an option for some stage 1A2 cancers with LVSI, with follow-up treatment available post-surgery. Fertility is preserved by observation or cone biopsy, not by extrafascial hysterectomy.

Lobectomy, a surgical procedure removing only the lobe containing a cancerous nodule, is an option for small, low-risk, non-invasive thyroid cancers that have not spread beyond the thyroid, especially if the patient has never had radiation therapy and the tumor is between 1 and 4 cm. It is performed under general anesthesia via a small neck incision and involves removing the isthmus. After lobectomy, short-term follow-up includes physical exams, TSH blood tests, and a neck ultrasound recommended 6 to 12 months post-surgery. Unlike total thyroidectomy, Tg testing is not useful after lobectomy. About one in three patients after lobectomy require thyroid hormone replacement therapy, typically with levothyroxine, to maintain TSH in the low normal range, with suppressed TSH levels used for higher-risk cancers or signs of recurrence. Long-term surveillance for patients with no evidence of disease includes physical exams, TSH tests, and periodic neck ultrasounds, with care team guidance on ultrasound frequency. In cases of NED, additional tests like CT or MRI may be used if recurrence is suspected.

A medical binder is a tool used to organize medical records, including copies of blood tests, imaging results, cancer reports, pathology reports, and other test types such as radiology and genetics. It includes folders for insurance forms, treatments, procedures, and test types, with items organized by date. The binder has a zipper pocket for a pen, small calendar, and insurance cards and may include a section for questions and notes. It is helpful for seeking a second opinion and is brought to doctor’s offices or hospitals. Patients can obtain copies of key records through online patient portals, which allow viewing and downloading of test results and other medical records to add to the binder. Other providers may request these records, and a medical binder supports access to comprehensive, organized information during medical care. Thom, a cancer survivor, used a notebook to record appointments and requested to record early visits for later review.

Clinical trials for cancer are surrounded by myths and misconceptions, and many cancer patients do not well understand the possible benefits and risks. Placebos, which are inactive versions of real medicines, are almost never used alone in cancer clinical trials; instead, patients may receive a placebo or a new drug in combination with standard treatment. Participants are always informed verbally and in writing before enrollment whether a placebo is part of the trial. A common concern is whether a patient will receive a placebo. Support groups, which include people at different stages of treatment such as newly diagnosed or those who have finished treatment, are found to be helpful for cancer patients. If support groups are not available at a hospital or community, individuals can check websites listed in a book to find them.

Advanced prostate cancer has multiple treatment options, including hormone therapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, radiation therapy, and surgery. Hormone therapy has been the main treatment for advanced prostate cancer for several decades and is often combined with other therapies, which are typically more effective than single therapies. Systemic therapies, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, work throughout the body and may be used alone or in combination. Personal and religious beliefs about treatment are important and should be shared with the care team. New tests and treatments are available, and patients are encouraged to seek care at a medical center specializing in prostate cancer. Chemical peels, which use trichloroacetic acid, are among other therapies used for actinic keratoses, not prostate cancer. Clinical trials have led to new treatments for bladder cancer, with improvements expected in the next few years.

Bone marrow tests, including bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, are bedside procedures that do not require an operating room and are typically performed on the pelvis, with the patient lying on their belly or side. An aspirate uses a hollow needle to draw liquid bone marrow into a syringe, while a biopsy uses a wider needle to remove a small piece of bone. Both procedures involve inserting a needle through the skin and into the bone, with the patient potentially experiencing bone pain at the hip for a few days and skin bruising. The samples are reviewed by a pathologist specializing in AML, who examines the overall appearance, size, shape, and type of cells, performing histology, histopathology, or hematopathology reviews. These tests are commonly performed together and may be indicated for diagnosing AML, BPDCN, or evaluating bone involvement in lymphoma. BPDCN can be found in blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, and skin, and if suspected, additional biopsies of lymph nodes or skin may be conducted. Bone marrow tests are not routinely needed for CLL but may be used to determine low blood cell counts.

A surgeon performs various procedures under general anesthesia, including sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB), where a radioactive and blue dye are injected into the skin to locate and remove lymph nodes for cancer staging and treatment. Plastic surgeons remove cancer, reconstruct, restore, and repair body parts, and are trained to close wounds, especially those involving deeper tissue, using techniques like linear closure, which reshapes wounds from circular to fusiform to enable linear stitching. Direct laryngoscopy, performed under general anesthesia in an operating room, uses a laryngoscope to examine the throat, take tissue samples, and determine if a primary tumor is resectable. Doctors may examine the bowel and bladder for cancer under general anesthesia, referred to as examinations under anesthesia (EUAs). If both bowel and bladder are removed, a double-barreled wet colostomy (DBWC) is used for both urinary and fecal diversion and has fewer leaks than separate diversions. The surgeon explains the recommended procedure in detail.

Chemotherapy regimens such as capecitabine and 5-FU/leucovorin, FOLFOX, and CAPEOX are recommended for high-risk stage 3 colon cancers, typically administered for 3 to 6 months depending on the regimen and recurrence risk. FOLFOX is given for 6 months, while CAPEOX is given for 3 months. Stage 3 chemotherapy is recommended after colectomy and may include chemoradiation, which uses 5-FU or capecitabine, though it is generally not recommended after modified DCF. Mitomycin is administered intravenously on the first day of capecitabine initiation and again at the start of week 5. 5-FU is delivered via a wearable pump connected to a central venous catheter for home administration or applied directly to skin. Capecitabine is taken orally twice daily, Monday through Friday during radiation, for 5.5 to 6 weeks. Hyperkeratosis, or thickening of the skin’s outer layer, is treated by softening and breaking down the top layer. Calcipotriene, a vitamin D form, is used with 5-FU to treat actinic keratosis.

Pain is a potential side effect of treatment, which may be life-threatening, lifelong, or irreversible after treatment ends. Patients can prevent or relieve side effects using medicines, which may also worsen some effects, and can be administered to manage symptoms. Side effects may last for varying durations, worsen or lessen over time, and require medical attention if signs appear. Patients are advised to call the doctor or text for guidance when side effects occur. An anesthesiologist performs a pre-anesthesia exam, including a physical check of the throat and airway, and administers anesthesia—caused by drugs—to prevent pain during procedures like surgery or endoscopies. A panendoscopy, performed under anesthesia, involves passing endoscopes through the mouth or nose to examine the mouth, oropharynx, larynx, esophagus, trachea, and bronchi, and may be done to detect tumors when cancer origin is unclear or lymph nodes appear abnormal. Bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy are specific endoscopic procedures performed under anesthesia to examine the airway and esophagus, respectively, and may include biopsies using tools passed through scopes.

Liver function tests (LFTs) assess liver health by measuring chemicals made or processed by the liver; abnormal levels indicate liver dysfunction, bile duct blockage, or cancer spread to the liver. Abnormal levels may also signal poor organ function or liver damage, especially when enzyme levels are too high or too low. LFTs are often performed alongside a blood chemistry profile, which measures chemicals affected by the kidneys, bones, and other organs and tissues; abnormal levels in the profile may indicate organ dysfunction, cancer spread, or diseases. The liver removes toxins from the blood and produces enzymes; enzyme levels that are too high or too low may indicate liver damage or cancer. Blood tests including LFTs, a blood chemistry profile, and a CBC are used to evaluate overall health and may guide treatment decisions based on protein and chemical levels.

Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) is a highly curable cancer that typically starts in lymph nodes of the upper body and is most commonly diagnosed between ages 15 and 30 or after age 55. It has two types, with classic Hodgkin lymphoma being the most common and identifiable by large, abnormal lymphocytes called Reed-Sternberg cells, which may have more than one nucleus. Classic HL has various subtypes but all receive the same care. HL has overlapping features with mediastinal gray zone lymphoma (MGZL), which shares characteristics with both primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma and HL, and MGZL is treated with chemotherapy. Information on HL in children and adolescents, including those aged 15 to 39 (AYAs), is available through NCCN.org/patientguidelines and the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. AYAs are defined by age at initial diagnosis, and pediatric categories include individuals 18 years or under, adolescents, and young adults. HL cells differ from other lymphomas under the microscope.

Genetic testing is recommended for everyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer to determine the presence of mutations in BRCA genes or other genes involved in hereditary cancer, including germline BRCA mutations. It is performed on normal tissue such as blood, saliva, or a cheek swab and can be conducted by a gynecology or oncology care team or a genetic counselor. Testing also includes tumor analysis for BRCA mutations and DNA repair-related genes. The doctor assesses hereditary ovarian cancer risk based on age, health, and family history. Hereditary ovarian cancer is most often caused by BRCA gene mutations, with Lynch syndrome being another cause. BRCA status influences decisions about maintenance therapy if initial treatment is successful. Ovarian cancer testing includes abdominal and pelvic exams, imaging, biopsy, family history, blood tests, and biomarker testing.

Invasive breast cancer occurs when cancerous cells grow outside the milk ducts or milk glands (lobules) into surrounding breast tissue or nearby lymph nodes. It spreads through lymph or blood to lymph nodes or other parts of the body. Ductal carcinoma, the most common type of breast cancer, begins in the cells lining milk ducts, while lobular carcinoma, the second most common, starts in the lobules (milk glands). Both ductal and lobular carcinomas can become invasive. Noninvasive cancer, such as DCIS, is confined to ducts or lobules. Stages 1, 2, and 3 are all invasive, meaning the cancer has grown beyond the ducts or lobules and may be present in axillary lymph nodes. Cancer cells from the breast can spread to nearby lymph nodes or distant organs via lymph or blood.

Methotrexate is an antimetabolite chemotherapy drug that blocks folate use, preventing lymphoma cells from multiplying. It is the most effective drug for primary CNS lymphoma and is used intrathecally to treat AML in the spinal fluid or brain. High-dose methotrexate is required to overcome the blood-brain barrier, which normally blocks chemotherapy drugs like methotrexate from reaching the brain. The blood-brain barrier protects the brain by preventing germs, infections, and toxins from entering. Dose-dense chemotherapy, a method that shortens time between treatments, is used to treat bladder cancer and includes methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin, and cisplatin (known as ddMVAC). Doxorubicin, an anthracycline, is also known as Adriamycin or Doxil. Fluorouracil is another antimetabolite used in chemotherapy.

MGZL has features of both classical Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin PMBL, with no standard treatment; it is typically treated with chemotherapy, and rituximab may be added if tumor cells are present, resulting in chemoimmunotherapy, with involved site radiation therapy possible for localized disease. The Guide provides treatment recommendations for common and rare ovarian cancers, noting they often arise in the epithelium or fallopian tube. For metastatic thyroid cancer not treatable by surgery or RAI, the Guide lists targeted therapies, with systemic therapies recommended if unavailable, and clinical trial participation strongly encouraged. Chapter 6 focuses on BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL, which involves an intensive combination of systemic therapies to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL protein caused by the BCR::ABL1 gene, and also discusses chordoma treatment and an aggressive subtype of AML. Systemic therapies include chemotherapy and immunotherapy, administered by medical oncologists. Tests for diagnosing chronic myeloid leukemia are described in the Guide.

N0 indicates no cancer in nearby lymph nodes, while N1 indicates cancer found in regional lymph nodes, which are located near the tumor. Nodal disease refers to cancer in lymph nodes and is rare in bone cancer. Higher N numbers (N1, N2, N3) correspond to more lymph nodes with metastases. M1 indicates distant metastasis, with M1a meaning lung metastasis and M1b meaning bone or other distant site metastasis. A TNM score of T4, N1, M1 means the tumor has grown outside the prostate (T4), spread to regional lymph nodes (N1), and metastasized to distant sites (M1). Cancer in lymph nodes is confirmed via needle biopsy. The higher the numbers in T or M, the larger the tumor or the more cancer has spread. Regional lymph nodes function as filters to fight infection and remove harmful substances.

The mouth, also known as the oral cavity or buccal cavity, is the first part of both the digestive and respiratory systems and consists of structures including the lips, cheeks, tongue, hard palate, gums, teeth, and alveolar ridge. It performs key functions such as eating, speaking, breathing, tasting, swallowing, and drinking. The oral mucosa lines the inside of the mouth and lips, composed of epithelium containing stratified squamous cells and lamina propria. Mouth cancer, primarily squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), arises in the surface epithelium of the oral cavity and can develop in the lips, gums, buccal mucosa, front two-thirds of the tongue, hard palate, alveolar ridge, floor of the mouth, and retromolar trigone. It is classified as a type of head and neck cancer.
