A tumor may grow through the layers of the oral mucosa and is considered unresectable if it cannot be safely removed due to involvement of critical structures. Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the vermilion lip is excluded from this context.

A complete head and neck exam includes examining the head and neck, with areas like the oropharynx (located inside the throat) not visible when the mouth is open. Healthcare providers use a special mirror or fiberoptic scope to view these areas. Radiation therapy to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands such as the thyroid and pituitary glands, located in the head and neck region, and blood tests to evaluate thyroid endocrine levels may be conducted before and/or after treatment. Radiation therapy is very effective for small tumors and for tumors in the head and neck. There are over 300 lymph nodes in the head and neck, and most tumors, including throat tumors, spread to nearby lymph nodes. A flexible cystoscope is used for viewing and biopsy, while a rigid cystoscope, though more invasive, can remove small tumors.

A comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) is a group of 14 blood tests that assesses organ function, including liver and kidney health, and measures blood sugar, calcium, and electrolyte levels. It is used to screen for many diseases and monitor treatment outcomes, particularly during AML treatment and recovery, where multiple blood tests are required to evaluate blood counts, organ function, and disease signs. A complete blood count (CBC) with differential measures red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, with the differential counting each type of white blood cell and checking for balance; high blast counts may indicate abnormal conditions like CLL. Abnormal CMP levels may suggest impaired liver or kidney function. Beta-2 microglobulin, released by B cells, is elevated in CLL and may indicate disease progression. Recovery after colectomy can involve side effects such as anastomotic leak, bowel habit changes, bowel obstruction, or hernia. Thom, an anal cancer survivor, emphasizes that recovery is challenging but manageable.

The stomach wall consists of five layers: mucosa (containing surface epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscle (also called muscularis propria, a type of soft tissue that helps move food), subserosa, and serosa, which covers the stomach and allows smooth movement. The mucosa, the innermost layer, is where cancer typically begins and where pre-cancerous changes occur; early-stage stomach cancer remains confined to this layer and does not involve lymph nodes. Locoregional cancer invades the submucosa or deeper layers and may involve regional lymph nodes. Cancer can grow inside the stomach, forming ulcers or masses, and spread via blood or lymphatic systems to distant sites such as the liver, abdominal lining, or distant lymph nodes. The lamina propria, a connective tissue layer beneath the epithelium, supports stomach glands that produce acid, enzymes, mucus, and hormones. Muscle is a type of soft tissue that includes muscles, nerves, tendons, blood, and lymph vessels.

NCCN.org/patientguidelines and the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app provide comprehensive patient resources on various cancer topics. Side effects of treatments, including nausea and vomiting, fatigue, and others, vary by drug, dose, treatment duration, and individual patient response, with the treatment team monitoring and managing them. Patients are encouraged to communicate bothersome side effects and ask about management options. Nausea and vomiting are specifically addressed in the NCCN Guidelines for Patients, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the app. Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), including mycosis fungoides, Sézary syndrome, and PCLPDs, develops from abnormal T cells and is covered in the guidelines. Information on fertility and family planning, including frozen ovarian tissue that can be reimplanted, is available in the NCCN Guidelines for Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer. Neuroendocrine tumor and esophageal cancer information is also available through the same resources. Immunotherapy side effects, including immune checkpoint inhibitors, are covered in dedicated NCCN patient guidelines.

Anal cancer treatment, particularly radiation therapy, can cause long-term side effects including bowel, urinary, and sexual function issues, with scar tissue forming due to tissue damage from radiation to the anus, affecting anal muscle function. Survivors may experience both short- and long-term health effects that vary by individual and treatments received. Nodules can result from cancer, infections, scar tissue, or other conditions and require expert evaluation if suspected to be cancerous. Cancer treatment centers offer programs focused on post-treatment sexual health, and patients are encouraged to ask their doctor for resources and information. Treatment teams provide guidance on foods to help with bowel changes and those to avoid, and survivors may benefit from consulting a dietitian specializing in the nutritional needs of anal cancer or digestive system cancer survivors. The pathologist determines if a nodule is cancerous and identifies the cancer type. Detailed treatment information is available in Part 2: Treatment Guide.

A primary care doctor advises on cancer screening based on sex, age, and risk level, including for breast, cervical, colorectal, and prostate cancer, and provides ongoing care after treatment. Patients should meet with a nutrition expert or nutritionist/dietitian before treatment to ensure adequate and sustained nutrition, with recommendations for foods and fluids. Nutrition assessment, blood tests, imaging tests, and endoscopy are part of stomach cancer testing. The treatment team monitors for weight loss and signs of inadequate nutrition during and after treatment. Radiation to the pelvis may weaken pelvic bones and increase fracture risk, prompting bone density monitoring. Patients may also receive immunizations like the flu shot, undergo blood pressure and hepatitis C screening, and discuss aspirin use with their doctor. Pelvic floor therapy, including Kegel exercises and hands-on techniques by a physical therapist, may be recommended.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients include a section called "Questions to Ask" at the end of each chapter, providing suggested questions to help patients gain information on all aspects of care. These questions assist individuals in understanding cancer care, discussing treatment options with their care team, and sharing concerns. Patients are encouraged to advocate for themselves by asking questions and making shared decisions, which increases satisfaction and reduces anxiety. Many people do not know what to ask their care team, making these suggested questions particularly valuable. Accurate testing is essential for diagnosing and treating ALL, which can be found in bone marrow, blood, testicles, and the central nervous system. In certain cases, a diagnosis of ALL can be made with less than 20 percent lymphoblasts. Seeking the opinion of an AML specialist can improve care outcomes.

Skin exams by a doctor are essential for monitoring local and regional squamous cell skin cancer (CSCC). For local CSCC, exams occur at least every 3 to 12 months (low-risk) or every 3 to 6 months (high-risk) during the first 2 years after treatment. If no further cancer develops, exams are spaced every 6 to 12 months for 3 years, then annually for life. For regional CSCC, which has spread to nearby lymph nodes, exams are every 2 to 3 months for 1 year, every 2 to 4 months for the second year, every 4 to 6 months for 3 years, then every 6 to 12 months for life. NCCN experts recommend annual exams for very high-risk local CSCC. Skin exams include a full body check and lymph node assessment, with patients undressing and wearing a paper gown. Exams are adjusted to allow full visibility. After treatment, ongoing vigilance is needed, especially for bladder cancer, which often returns for the rest of a patient’s life.

Blood is a tissue composed of cells that work together to transport oxygen and nutrients, carry away waste, support the immune system, and prevent bleeding. It has four main components: plasma, red blood cells (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leukocytes), and platelets (thrombocytes). Plasma is a clear yellowish fluid primarily composed of water and serves as the medium in which blood cells float. Red blood cells carry oxygen throughout the body. White blood cells fight infections and include granulocytes (such as neutrophils), monocytes, and lymphocytes. Platelets help control bleeding. Blood cells are continuously replaced in the body, originating from blood stem cells in bone marrow, which can develop into red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a type of blood cancer.

Anal tumors between 2 cm and 5 cm are classified as stage IIA with staging description T2, N0, M0. Tumors larger than 5 cm are classified as stage IIB with staging description T3, N0, M0. T3 tumors exceed 5 cm in size or are confined to four or more adjacent or nonadjacent vertebrae, or indicate more than one tumor in the primary bone site. T4 tumors are any size and have invaded nearby structures such as the chest wall or skin of the breast. Stage IIIA involves tumors 5 cm or smaller with cancer in nearby lymph nodes (staging T1/N1/M0 or T2/N1/M0). Stage IIIB involves tumor invasion of nearby organs without lymph node involvement (T4/N0/M0). Stage IIIC includes tumors larger than 5 cm or with organ invasion and lymph node spread (T3 or T4 with N1/M0).

Targeted therapy is a form of systemic therapy that focuses on specific features of cancer cells, such as their growth, division, and movement, by stopping the action of molecules that help cancer cells grow and survive. It is most effective for cancers with biomarkers and is used for recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer with specific biomarkers. Gemtuzumab ozogamicin (GO) is a targeted therapy linked to a chemotherapy drug. Targeted therapy is preferred for cancer that cannot be surgically removed and is progressing, with lenvatinib (Lenvima) as the first-line option, followed by sorafenib (Nexavar); if cancer worsens after these, cabozantinib (Cabometyx) is recommended. Targeted therapy may also be used for cervical cancer that returns or spreads after chemotherapy. It attacks specific parts of cancer cells to slow their growth and spread. Systemic therapy, which includes chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, uses medicines that travel through the bloodstream to affect cells throughout the body.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a sexually transmitted virus that infects surface cells of skin and moist surfaces, including the cervix, vagina, vulva, penis, anus, mouth, and throat. Most HPV infections clear on their own, but can cause abnormal tissue growth known as warts or lead to HPV-related cancer. High-risk HPV types, such as HPV16, are linked to cancers including cervical, vulvar, vaginal, anal, and throat cancers. The strongest risk factor for anal cancer is long-term HPV infection, with other risk factors including HIV, immunosuppressant use, smoking, a history of anal sex or sexually transmitted infections, and certain autoimmune disorders like Crohn’s disease. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type of anal cancer, originating in the anal canal or perianal region. HPV infection can also cause warts on the anus or genitals. A weakened immune system increases the risk of persistent HPV infection and related cancers.

A stereotactic biopsy is a precise surgical procedure performed by a neurosurgeon in the operating room to diagnose brain tumors, particularly gliomas or primary CNS lymphoma, when the tumor is in a hard-to-reach or vital area. It begins with fitting the patient with a frame or tiny markers around the head, followed by anesthesia and trimming a small area of hair to the scalp. The neurosurgeon makes a small opening in the skull, inserts a thin hollow needle into the brain, and removes a sliver of tumor tissue. A computerized navigation system, connected to MRI or CT imaging, enables high-precision targeting. The removed tissue is sent to a lab for testing to detect cancer cells. This procedure aims to remove only enough tissue for diagnosis, avoiding extensive surgery. After the procedure, the scalp opening is closed with sutures, and the patient may go home the next day. Stereotactic biopsy is required to confirm diagnoses and guide further treatment.

Flow cytometry is a laboratory method that detects, identifies, and counts specific cells by passing them through a beam of light after adding a light-sensitive dye; it measures cell number, size, and shape and can be performed on circulating blood or bone marrow aspirate. It is most commonly used for immunophenotyping, which uses antibodies to detect white blood cell antigens (biomarkers) on the cell surface. Unlike a blood test, which can only count white blood cells and cannot detect subtle differences between blood cancers, flow cytometry can detect these differences. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), a slow-growing blood cancer, is confirmed by a blood test showing at least 5,000 monoclonal B lymphocytes per microliter and is evaluated by a hematopathologist, an expert in diagnosing blood and immune cell cancers. CLL may not require treatment for years, and for those who do, newer treatments help extend life. A blood smear is also examined by hematopathologists and oncologists to identify abnormal cells that may indicate cancer type.

A biopsy removes tissue or fluid from the body to detect cancer, often during initial surgery or before surgery if cancer has spread widely. Tissue samples are sent to a lab where a pathologist examines them under a microscope to identify cancer cells and notes their appearance and other features. The pathologist determines how many core samples contain cancer and measures the percentage of cancer in each. For certain cancers like throat cancer, the presence of the p16 protein is tested to detect HPV infection, which is key to staging and treatment decisions. The pathology report records the type and features of the biopsied samples, reveals the tumor type, and is used by the care team to plan treatment and predict disease course. The report is also provided for personal records. Biopsies may be guided by imaging such as mammogram, ultrasound, or MRI and may target the primary tumor or other tumors, including tissue from the breast or lymph nodes.

BEST CARE is achieved by advocating for oneself or one's child, asking questions, and making shared decisions with the care team. Patients who advocate for themselves are more likely to receive the care they want, especially when they understand test results and engage in shared decisions involving the healthcare team. Advocacy, asking questions, and participation in decision-making increase the likelihood of receiving desired care. Shared decisions involve collaboration between the patient and the care team, and patients should actively ask questions about test results and treatment options. These actions collectively support patients in playing an active role in their care and achieving the care they desire.

Follicular lymphoma (FL) is a slow-growing, indolent type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) that arises from mature B cells and forms tumors in lymph nodes, often as clusters (follicles) in germinal centers. It can also appear in other tissues, including the bone marrow, where it is termed extranodal disease. FL may be detected through swollen lymph nodes or an enlarged spleen, commonly found in the neck, armpit, groin, chest, abdomen, or pelvis. Symptoms include fever, night sweats, fatigue, and weight loss, which are part of B symptoms. Diagnosis requires a range of tests, including general health assessments, blood tests, biopsy, immunophenotyping, biomarker and genetic change testing, imaging, and heart tests. Fertility assessments are required for all genders, and pregnancy prevention is necessary during treatment. Not everyone with FL requires immediate treatment.

Cirrhosis is a liver condition caused by hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, alcohol use, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, genetic hemochromatosis, stage 4 primary biliary cholangitis, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, or other factors. Individuals with cirrhosis should be screened for liver cancer and enrolled in a liver cancer screening program, especially those with chronic hepatitis B. Risk factors for liver cancer in those with cirrhosis include hepatitis B or C, alcohol use, NAFLD, and other causes of cirrhosis. Hepatitis B and C are blood- and bodily fluid-transmitted viruses that can cause chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, liver failure, and liver cancer. Cancer treatments, including chemotherapy, can reactivate hepatitis B or C, causing liver harm, and may reduce fertility or cause birth defects. Patients on chemotherapy should avoid pregnancy, and dental work may be recommended before treatment. Hepatitis B and C screening tests determine past or current infection status.

Surgical menopause occurs when both ovaries are removed during surgery, causing a sudden drop in estrogen, which leads to symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleeping problems, weight gain, mood changes, and vaginal atrophy—characterized by vaginal thinning, drying, and irritation. This condition is more sudden and severe than natural menopause and carries long-term risks including cardiovascular disease and osteoporosis. Symptoms are common in individuals who have not yet entered menopause. Surgical risks include pain, swelling, scars, leg swelling, urinary issues, and constipation, especially in ovarian cancer surgery. Recent abdominal surgery or cancer increases the risk of blood clots, also known as deep vein thrombosis. A doctor may recommend non-hormonal medicine or hormone replacement therapy (HRT), now more commonly referred to as menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), especially after radiation therapy. HRT is not the same as endocrine therapy and is used to manage symptoms of surgical or radiation-induced menopause. Consultation with a menopausal symptom team is advised to determine suitability.

Microsatellites are short, repeated strings of DNA. Errors in these sequences are fixed by mismatch repair (MMR) proteins; when DNA mutations prevent this repair, errors accumulate, leading to microsatellite instability (MSI) or deficient mismatch repair (dMMR). This condition, known as MSI-H, occurs when cancer cells have more than a normal number of microsatellites and is typically caused by mutations in MMR genes, such as DMMR genes. MSI-H is a biomarker used in cancer diagnosis and treatment guidance, particularly in rectal and colon cancers, where tumor testing for MMR gene mutations is required. An abnormal result is classified as either dMMR or MSI-H, while tumors without these changes are termed microsatellite stable (MSS) or mismatch repair proficient (pMMR). If a cancer is dMMR/MSI-H, patients are tested for inherited mutations in MMR genes.

Loss of appetite, hair loss, mouth sores, constipation, diarrhea, and low blood cell counts (including white cells, red cells, and platelets) are common side effects of both chemotherapy and systemic therapy. These effects are primarily caused by the death of fast-growing cells in the intestines, mouth, and blood. Immune-related adverse events (irAEs), which can occur with immunotherapy, include fatigue, nausea, loss of appetite, mouth sores, constipation, diarrhea, low blood cell counts, lung and breathing problems (such as cough, shortness of breath, and chest pain), organ damage (liver and kidneys), rash, body aches, and high blood pressure. Some targeted therapies may cause serious side effects affecting the heart, skin, or digestive system. Long-term side effects of systemic therapy may include other cancers, heart disease, or infertility. Patients should ask their care team for a complete list of potential side effects, and information is available through NCCN.org/patientguidelines and the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app.

A tumor biopsy sample is tested for estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), HER2 status, and grade to guide treatment. HER2 is a protein involved in normal cell growth; in some breast cancers, it is present in higher amounts, leading to HER2-positive breast cancer. Progesterone receptor binds progesterone and provides survival and proliferation signals, with PR expression suggesting estrogen dependence. Systemic treatment, based on ER, PR, and HER2 expression, is used to shrink tumors in inflammatory breast cancer and may continue even if surgery is not possible. Systemic therapy includes HER2 inhibitors, which block growth signals from HER2 inside the cell, and HER2 antibodies, which prevent external growth signals and enhance immune attack on cancer cells. Antibody drug conjugates target HER2, deliver chemotherapy into cancer cells, and are used in HER2-positive cancers. These tests and treatments help detect cancer, plan therapy, and assess treatment effectiveness.

Abdominal surgery is recommended for T1 tumors and some T3 cancers that have not spread to lymph nodes, involving cutting into the abdomen to remove the rectal tumor, surrounding healthy tissue, and nearby lymph nodes. At least 12 lymph nodes are removed near the tumor and tested for cancer; a pathologist examines the tissue to determine how far the cancer has grown in the rectal wall and assigns a stage, which guides chemotherapy decisions. The procedure depends on tumor location and extent, with transabdominal surgery including low anterior resection (LAR) for mid to upper rectum tumors, which removes the rectal tumor and last section of the colon, possibly connecting the colon to the rectum or anus. For T1 tumors at the rectum's end, transanal local excision is an alternative that removes cancer and surrounding tissue without lymph node removal. Cancer starts in the innermost layer of the rectal wall, which contacts stool, and can grow through layers, invade pelvic structures, or spread to other organs. MRI may detect abdominal or liver cancer and assess tumor depth and lymph node spread, especially when contrast is not possible.

A urologist, an expert in the urinary system and male reproductive organs, performs a prostate biopsy to evaluate prostate cancer. The procedure involves inserting a hollow needle through the perineum or rectum, guided by ultrasound imaging or combined MRI and ultrasound images, to obtain a core sample of prostate tissue. Each core sample is 1 to 2 millimeters wide and 12 to 20 millimeters long, roughly the size of a toothpick and a raisin. The urologist typically takes 12 or more core samples from different parts of the prostate to provide a comprehensive evaluation of cancer. The needle is inserted into the prostate gland using a lubricated probe inserted into the rectum, which provides a visual image of the gland. The patient is given anesthesia to numb pain or induce sleep and lies on their side or back. The biopsy is guided by ultrasound, which creates a view of the prostate using high-energy sound waves, and does not require opening the abdomen. The procedure may also involve sampling from metastasis if diagnosed.

A sugar radiotracer is injected into a vein about an hour before a PET scan, where it emits detectable energy to show areas of high sugar uptake, such as cancer cells, which appear as bright spots. While PET scans are effective at detecting small groups of cancer cells and may help identify ovarian cancer spread, not all bright spots indicate cancer; inflammation or infection can also appear as bright spots. The heart, brain, kidneys, and bladder can be bright on PET scans due to normal metabolic activity. Electrolytes are essential ions that support the proper functioning of nerves, muscles, and the heart by facilitating nutrient transport and waste removal. Before and during trastuzumab treatment, the heart is monitored using tests that measure left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), which quantifies the amount of blood pumped from the left side of the heart. The part of the chest that holds the heart and separates the lungs also contains the sternum and is home to mediastinal lymphomas.

Resection, the surgical removal of a larger piece of the rectum, may be needed after polypectomy based on the size and shape of the polyp, polypectomy results, and testing of the removed tissue. Pedunculated polyps are mushroom-shaped, have a stalk and round top, and stick out from the colon wall, while sessile polyps are flat, lack a stalk, and are more likely to return after treatment. Sessile polyps require imaging with endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) or pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to guide surgical decisions. A polyp in which cancer has just started to grow is called a malignant polyp. Providers review test results with patients, discuss treatment options, and make decisions about resection. Radiation therapy is an option after resection, for those who cannot or choose not to have surgery.

Corticosteroids, commonly known as steroids, are used to shrink lymphomas and reduce brain swelling in primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma, rapidly alleviating symptoms, but are only administered for a short duration—typically in newly diagnosed patients—due to loss of effectiveness and side effects with long-term use. Steroids should not begin until after biopsy and diagnosis to avoid altering lymphoma cell appearance, which could hinder accurate diagnosis. Side effects include increased hunger, sleep disturbances, slow wound healing, stomach upset, mood changes, and swelling in ankles, feet, and hands; most resolve after discontinuation. Steroids and anti-androgens, androgen synthesis inhibitors are available as pills taken 1 to 3 times daily. Treatment for CNS lymphoma includes corticosteroids, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell rescue, with chemotherapy essential for stem cell rescue. Surgery is not recommended due to risks. NCCN experts recommend all patients consider joining a clinical trial, which is a type of research study. Treatment is personalized, with no single best option, and therapies are often combined. Systemic therapies, including oral pills, affect both cancer and normal cells and may cause side effects.

Tumor mutation testing uses a sample of tumor or blood to detect specific DNA mutations, protein levels, and other molecular features in cancer cells, differing from inherited genetic testing, which assesses mutations from biological parents. It tests only the tumor, not the rest of the body. Detected DNA mutations and protein levels can be targeted with specific therapies. Certain mutations, such as PIK3CA, are specifically targetable with therapies. The testing helps identify actionable alterations that may guide treatment decisions.

Rituximab (also known as Rituxan) is a monoclonal antibody used as the main immunotherapy drug for primary CNS lymphoma. It targets CD20 proteins on the surface of cancerous and some healthy blood cells, helping the immune system locate and destroy cancer cells. Administered via IV infusion, rituximab may cause side effects such as drowsiness, fatigue, joint pain, loss of appetite, low blood cell counts, serious blood clots, and rashes. It is most effective when combined with chemotherapy, particularly in induction therapy, where it is given with high-dose methotrexate. High-dose methotrexate is the preferred induction therapy for primary CNS lymphoma but is not suitable for patients with kidney issues, those with cancer in the spine or spinal fluid, or those who cannot tolerate it. Alternative induction therapies may include temozolomide, ibrutinib, lenalidomide, or other agents. Patients are advised to track symptoms and side effects using a weekly diary, calendar, smartphone app, or personal recording method.

Clinical trials are free to enroll in, with study sponsors covering research-related costs like the study drug, though participants may incur indirect costs such as transportation or child care. Standard cancer care continues during trials and is typically covered by insurance, with patients responsible for copays and uncovered costs. Placebos are rarely used alone in cancer trials and are usually combined with standard treatment or a new drug; participants are informed verbally and in writing if a placebo is included. In the United States, patients can find clinical trials through NCCN Cancer Centers at NCCN.org/cancercenters or via the NCI’s search tool at cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/clinical-trials/search. Worldwide, the U.S. National Library of Medicine (NLM) provides access to clinicaltrials.gov. If help is needed, the NCI’s Cancer Information Service (CIS) can be contacted at CANCER (6237) or via cancer.gov/contact.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer in non-smokers and accounts for 4 out of 10 non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC), originating in mucus-producing cells of the alveoli. It is also the most common type of colon cancer, arising from glandular cells in adenomas, which are the most common type of polyp and adrenal gland tumor (adrenocortical adenoma). Adenomas are noncancerous, may not require treatment if small and asymptomatic, and can develop into invasive colon cancer over years. Adenocarcinoma forms when cancer starts in an adenoma and is the primary type of colorectal cancer. Large cell carcinoma, another NSCLC subtype, begins in large cells and accounts for 5 out of 10 NSCLCs. Squamous cell carcinoma starts in flat cells lining the bronchi and accounts for 3 out of 10 NSCLCs. Adenomas that overproduce aldosterone or cortisol are called aldosteronomas or cause Cushing syndrome, respectively.

The TNM system stages cancer based on tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M). Primary tumor size is measured in centimeters or millimeters, with a large pea approximating 1 cm, a golf ball approximating 4 cm, and a baseball approximating 7 cm. Tumor micrometastasis is smaller than 1 mm and may be written as T1mi. Higher numbers in the T component indicate larger tumors or more spread cancer. The TNM score helps determine the extent of cancer and assess risk for spread, which in turn guides treatment decisions. Tumor size is also measured in centimeters for head and neck tumors, and one inch equals 2.54 cm. Ipsilateral means on the same side of the body.

The uterus is where a baby grows and develops, with the cervix at its lower end, which opens during birth to allow the baby into the vagina. Fallopian tubes, located on each side of the uterus, connect to its top and transport eggs from the ovaries to the uterus. A trachelectomy removes only the cervix and may also remove the upper vagina or pelvic lymph nodes; it is a fertility-sparing surgery because the uterus and ovaries remain intact, enabling future natural pregnancy. Simple trachelectomy removes only the cervix, while radical trachelectomy removes about 2 centimeters of vaginal tissue. Fertility-sparing surgery may remove ovaries and fallopian tubes but preserves the uterus. A tandem and ring applicator consists of a tandem tube that extends into the uterus and a ring that stays in the vagina and presses against the cervix, used in HDR brachytherapy. A tandem and ovoid applicator replaces the ring with hollow, rounded capsules. Removal of the uterus prevents pregnancy, while surgery aimed at cancer removal may also remove ovaries, fallopian tubes, and the uterus.

Calcium is essential for healthy teeth, bones, and body tissues, and its levels in the bloodstream are regulated by the parathyroid glands, which are located on the back of the thyroid gland. Elevated calcium levels, known as hypercalcemia, can indicate disease and are detected via a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP). Alkaline phosphatase (ALP), an enzyme in blood, may signal bone tumors, liver disorders, or pregnancy, potentially leading to a bone scan if levels are high. Blood tests assess organ function and detect disease by analyzing blood samples obtained via a needle inserted into a vein in the arm. A complete blood count (CBC) measures red blood cells (RBCs), which carry oxygen, white blood cells (WBCs), which include monocytes and fight infection, and platelets, which control bleeding. Blood also transports oxygen and nutrients, removes waste, and supports the immune system. Bone damage from cancer can cause calcium release into the bloodstream, leading to illness.

Precancerous changes occur in the inner lining (mucosa) of both the esophagus and stomach, often going undetected and causing no symptoms. Esophageal cancer develops slowly over years, starting when abnormal cells grow out of control in the mucosa layer of the esophagus wall, which has four layers including the mucosa in contact with food. Early-stage esophageal cancer is confined to the esophagus, may be 2 centimeters or smaller, and is not present in lymph nodes. Locoregional esophageal cancer has invaded the esophagus wall and spread to nearby lymph nodes or organs in direct contact with the esophagus. Early-stage stomach cancer similarly remains within the mucosa layer, is small (2 cm or less), and lacks lymph node involvement. Cancer may spread to lymphatic vessels, blood vessels, lymph nodes, or distant sites like the liver, lung, bone, or brain. Cancer care uses the metric system, including centimeters and millimeters, for treatment measurements.

Bevacizumab (Avastin) is used in the treatment of recurrent ovarian cancer, particularly when added to chemotherapy to inhibit the growth of new blood vessels feeding the tumor. It is recommended for stage 2, 3, and 4 ovarian cancers after surgery, typically in combination with paclitaxel and carboplatin given every 3 weeks for six cycles. If this regimen is not feasible, bevacizumab may be added. For platinum-resistant recurrent cancer—defined as no improvement or recurrence within 6 months of platinum-based therapy—non-platinum chemotherapy or bevacizumab is preferred. Tumors with folate receptor alpha (FRα) biomarker are treated with mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx, an antibody drug conjugate. Bevacizumab may be used alone as maintenance therapy for cancers without BRCA mutations or with unknown BRCA status, especially if it was part of the initial recurrence regimen. Before recurrence treatment, secondary cytoreductive surgery may be suggested to remove visible cancer. Treatment plans may vary based on medical conditions and overall health, and clinical trial enrollment is encouraged.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a common sexually transmitted infection affecting almost all sexually active individuals, with most people unaware of infection. In most cases, the immune system clears HPV, but in some, it causes long-term cell changes that can progress to cancer decades later. High-risk HPV strains, including HPV16 and HPV-Other, are more likely to lead to cancer. HPV is the primary cause of cervical, anal, penile, vaginal, and vulvar cancers, and is strongly linked to cervical and anal cancer. Long-term HPV infection is a key risk factor for these cancers, with progression to cancer often occurring decades after initial infection. In throat cancer, overexpression of p16 indicates HPV causation. Doctors are still studying why some individuals develop cancer while others do not. There are over 100 HPV strains, with certain types more likely to cause abnormal growths like warts on the anus, genitals, or body.

Creatinine, a waste product produced in muscles at a fixed rate based on muscle mass, is filtered by the kidneys and its level in the blood indicates kidney function; higher levels suggest reduced kidney function. Blood urea nitrogen (BUN), another waste product filtered by the kidneys, can also indicate impaired kidney function. A kidney function test measures these waste products to assess kidney health and guide treatment. The comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) measures substances in the blood, providing information about kidney and liver function. Hemoglobin (HGB) measures oxygen-carrying capacity in blood and may indicate the need for a red blood cell transfusion. Platelets prevent or stop bleeding by forming clots. Blasts, sometimes detected as a percentage of cells, may indicate leukemia. The pelvic floor consists of muscles that support pelvic organs and are essential for bowel and bladder control, sexual function, and arousal; pelvic floor physical therapy strengthens these muscles.

The stomach is a hollow organ located between the esophagus and small intestine, measuring 10 to 12 inches when empty. It secretes enzymes and acid to convert food and drink into chyme and serves as a temporary holding chamber. Part of the digestive system, it is made up of five main layers, including the inner and outer membranes. The inner membrane, known as the mucosa, is in direct contact with food. The outer membrane covers the external surface. The stomach is part of the GI tract, which includes the stomach, small bowel, and large bowel (rectum and colon). An upper endoscopy examines the upper GI tract by guiding a scope down the throat into the esophagus, stomach, and small bowel. Lymph nodes are found along the lesser and greater curvatures of the stomach.

A risk factor increases the likelihood of developing a disease or getting cancer. Having an impaired immune system is a risk factor for developing primary CNS lymphoma. Age is the biggest risk factor for prostate cancer. Risk factors do not guarantee disease development, as some individuals with risk factors do not develop the disease, and some without risk factors may still develop it. Risk factors increase the chance of developing cancer or getting a disease, and while they do not cause disease directly, they contribute to the probability. Primary CNS lymphoma is treated with chemotherapy, radiation therapy, stem cell transplant, or a combination of these treatments, and patients may also receive treatment in a clinical trial.

Patients with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) are encouraged to advocate for themselves by asking questions and making shared decisions with their care team, increasing the likelihood of receiving desired care. Seeking the opinion of a CML specialist is recommended to improve understanding of the condition and treatment options, and the NCCN Guidelines for Patients can support this understanding. When patients have better knowledge, they are better able to discuss their care and share concerns. Playing an active role in care leads to feeling more satisfied, a benefit reported by many people. This active involvement is a key factor in enhancing patient satisfaction and engagement in their health management.

Ejection fraction measures the amount of blood pumped out of the left side of the heart with each beat; a lower-than-normal ejection fraction indicates decreased heart function. Heart or cardiac tests are used to evaluate heart function, monitor treatment side effects, and assess heart function before treatment begins. These tests may lead to a referral to a cardiologist, a heart specialist. Patients should seek clarification if a doctor's explanation is unclear, as asking for simpler terms is a way of advocating for oneself. The left side of the heart pumps blood, and understanding one's medical condition is essential for informed care.

The digital rectal exam (DRE), also known as a prostate exam, is a simple, direct physical examination where a doctor inserts a gloved finger into the rectum to feel the prostate for irregularities or hard areas, which could indicate a tumor. It cannot feel all parts of the prostate and is typically combined with a PSA test and other factors like age, race, and family history to assess prostate health and determine if further testing is needed. The PSA test measures total PSA in nanograms per milliliter of blood and is used to evaluate prostate health and detect possible prostate cancer. Both tests are common in screening undiagnosed individuals and monitoring diagnosed cases. Factors such as race, age, and family history influence the likelihood of prostate cancer and are considered when deciding on further diagnostic steps like biopsy or imaging. Testing for prostate cancer is necessary to determine presence, stage, and to help plan treatment.

Primary CNS lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that arises from lymphocytes, abnormal white blood cells, and most commonly affects the central part of the brain, though it can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, or eyes. It exerts pressure on the central nervous system, leading to neurological symptoms such as leg or arm weakness, coordination or movement problems, personality changes, depression, confusion, memory problems, loss of bladder control, difficulty speaking or swallowing, headaches, nausea, vomiting, seizures, blurred or double vision. Diagnosis requires a neurological exam, imaging (MRI or CT), and biopsy. Primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoma (CBCL), a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL), appears as skin papules or nodules and is typically indolent; it is not skin cancer. Treatment options for specific CBCL subtypes are available through NCCN Guidelines for Patients.

Fertility-sparing treatment is an option for small, early-stage cancers (including stage 1 cervical cancer) that are limited to the cervix, involving surgery that does not remove the uterus or ovaries, thus allowing natural pregnancy in the future. This treatment is typically recommended for patients who wish to preserve fertility and is only available for early-stage cancers. If cancer is in both ovaries, a bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO) may be performed, which prevents natural pregnancy but allows pregnancy via assisted reproductive approaches like IVF. IVF involves fertilizing patient or donor eggs with sperm in a lab to create embryos, which are then implanted into the uterus or frozen for future use. Donor eggs are obtained from women undergoing hormone treatment to stimulate egg production. A unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (USO), performed when cancer is in one ovary, may preserve natural pregnancy if menopause has not occurred. External beam radiation therapy damages the ovaries and stops hormone production, impairing natural pregnancy.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients cover topics including about Hodgkin lymphoma, testing, staging, treatment for classic and nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, refractory or relapsed cases, and when treatment ends, along with other resources, words to know, and contributor listings. These guidelines help patients understand cancer care, enabling them to discuss care with their care team and share concerns. They also include information on fertility preservation and family planning, particularly relevant for adolescent and young adult cancer patients, with fertility specialists able to determine the best approach based on individual circumstances. The guidelines are available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and through the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app, which provides access to the full content and supports patient engagement in care decisions.

Metastatic anal cancer is primarily treated with chemotherapy or immunotherapy, often with enrollment in a clinical trial if available; it most commonly spreads to the liver or lungs and aims to help patients live longer and manage symptoms. Metastatic bladder cancer is treated with chemotherapy or immunotherapy, either alone or in combination, with the preferred combination therapy including Padcev (an antibody-drug conjugate targeting Nectin-4) and Keytruda (immunotherapy), combining targeted therapy and immunotherapy. For less advanced bladder cancer, a minor surgical procedure removes only the tumor, while more advanced cases may require entire bladder removal. Chemotherapy can be delivered directly into the bladder and is sometimes the main treatment without surgery. Treatment for both cancers depends on cancer stage, overall health, and personal preferences, and patients share symptom tracking information with their treatment team to improve symptom management.

An MRI scan lasts 1 to 2 hours, including 30 to 60 minutes of actual scanning time, and requires the patient to remain motionless throughout. Pillows or bolsters may be used to help maintain stillness. Metal objects, including jewelry, cell phones, wristwatches, and belts with metal buckles, are prohibited in the imaging room due to the strong magnetic fields. The scan uses radio waves and powerful magnets to create detailed images of the body, particularly useful for detecting prostate cancer, assessing spread to nearby lymph nodes or bones, and evaluating treatment effectiveness or recurrence. A contrast agent may be injected to enhance visibility of blood vessels, organs, and tissues, and is flushed out in urine. Patients with pacemakers, heart monitors, or certain surgical clips cannot undergo MRI. If a patient experiences nervousness in small spaces, they may be given a sedative to help relax. The appointment may occur before, during, or after a biopsy or cancer treatment.

Rectal tumors should be tested for mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR) or high microsatellite instability (MSI-H); cancers with dMMR should undergo Lynch syndrome testing, while those without are classified as mismatch repair proficient (pMMR) or microsatellite stable (MSS). Everyone with rectal cancer should have their family health history reviewed. MRI of the pelvis assesses cancer extent in the rectum and nearby lymph nodes, while CT of the chest and abdomen determines if cancer has spread to the liver, lungs, or other organs. Patients should inform their care team about fertility options, and doctors will provide information on fertility-related treatment risks and preservation options. Biopsies must be performed by an experienced surgeon at the cancer center where treatment is received. Reputable sites offer medically reviewed patient/caregiver information and resources, which are more reliable than random Google results. Resources on page 61 help locate an experienced surgeon and a treatment center, and assist in finding a new doctor if a patient moves after treatment.

The skin is the body’s largest organ, protecting against microbes, chemicals, and invaders, and enabling sensations of touch, heat, and cold while helping regulate body temperature. Squamous cell skin cancer (CSCC) begins in squamous cells found in the skin’s top layer, lungs, thyroid, and esophagus, often starting as scaly patches that become solid and misshapen. Radiation therapy is generally avoided in individuals with genetic conditions or connective tissue diseases like lupus or scleroderma, as these increase the risk of radiation-induced skin cancer, and repeated radiation to the same area is not recommended. Pheochromocytoma, a tumor originating in the adrenal medulla, is characterized by high blood pressure, headache, rapid heartbeat, and sweating; most are benign but can be cancerous. Malignant adrenal tumors are cancerous and rare, with about 300 to 500 diagnoses annually, and certain genetic conditions may increase the risk for these tumors.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common type of primary liver cancer, with secondary liver cancer occurring when other cancers spread to the liver, typically to the lung or bone. Risk factors for liver cancer include chronic hepatitis B, cirrhosis, NAFLD, diabetes, high weight, high cholesterol, and conditions affecting sugar processing. Screening, involving two tests every six months, is recommended for individuals at risk, such as those with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B, to detect liver cancer early when treatment is more likely to be curative. The goal of screening is to identify liver cancer in at-risk individuals before symptoms appear. HCC rarely spreads to nearby lymph nodes. Treatment options may be used for other cancers, carry risks and side effects that are managed through control strategies, and may require follow-up care or financial assistance. Clinical trials may offer new treatments but involve costs and durations, and alternative treatments are available if the primary one fails.

Patients should bring a friend, family member, or peer to doctor visits, write down questions and take notes during appointments, and ask their care team questions to better understand test results. They should obtain copies of blood tests, imaging results, and reports about their specific type of cancer and organize medical records, insurance forms, and test results into physical and digital files, including a medical binder with compartments for insurance cards, a pen, and a calendar. A contact list for the care team—including details about the specific cancer, treatment, and dates—should be maintained, updated, and kept in an accessible location such as a refrigerator or phone. Copies of medical documents are to be made for use in seeking a second opinion. Imaging tests often detect kidney cancer by chance, and further testing like biopsy or imaging studies helps determine the treatment plan based on test results. Patients should inform their primary care physician of changes to the contact list.

The narrator experienced discomfort in their bra, sharp shooting pains, and noticed changes in skin appearance, leading to a diagnosis of inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) without a visible lump, a fact clarified by a nurse. They underwent multiple office visits and discovered a small hard pebble under the skin, which later they realized changed their life and may have saved their life. The narrator’s dad was diagnosed with stomach cancer in 2013 and told he had only six months to live; the family was devastated, but they formed a team of experts that helped him achieve clinical cure. The narrator advises newly diagnosed individuals to be their own advocates and find a support community. Medical oncologists specialize in prescribing chemotherapy, which can be taken by mouth, injected, or intravenously, and work with gynecologic oncologists to plan treatment for ovarian cancer. Radiation oncologists are trained to use radiation therapy.

A hearing test, performed as needed, determines the presence, type, severity, and possible cause of hearing loss, with results displayed on an audiometer. Hearing loss can result from head and neck tumors or their treatment. Additional evaluations include a mirror exam, depression screen, nasopharyngeal fiberoptic exam, biopsy if needed, MRI from collarbone to skull base, CT of skull base and neck, FDG-PET/CT or chest CT for metastases, EBV DNA testing, dental exam, nutrition and speech/swallowing evaluation, eye and endocrine assessment, smoking cessation support, and fertility counseling. Iron is essential for hemoglobin production and oxygen transport in blood; iron deficiency may be monitored and treated with IV iron if needed, while iron overload is possible and must be managed under doctor supervision. Speech or swallowing therapists assess swallowing and speaking ability before and after treatment.

Metastatic disease refers to cancer that has spread to distant parts of the body, far from the primary site, and is distinct from regional spread, which involves nearby lymph nodes. Squamous cell skin cancer spreading to nearby lymph nodes is termed regional. Testing for disease spread includes scans of the upper body, stomach, and pelvis to detect metastatic disease. Benign adrenal tumors do not metastasize and are often found incidentally during imaging for unrelated issues, while functional adrenal tumors are usually benign but can become cancerous and spread. Cancer cells break away from a tumor, spread to other areas, and form new tumors. Ovarian cancer may cause noticeable body changes, with symptoms appearing only after the tumor has grown large or cancer has spread. Stomach cancers are grouped into three main categories based on how far the cancer has spread. Kidney cancer has spread to distant parts of the body, confirming metastatic disease. A biopsy does not cause prostate cancer to spread or worsen.

Antigens are proteins found on the surface or inside white blood cells and are used in immunohistochemistry (IHC), a staining process that involves adding a chemical marker to cells. IHC is used to study cells and identify their immunophenotype in biopsy or tissue samples, particularly in cancer diagnosis. The process is studied under a microscope, where pathologists examine tumor tissue to note its appearance, other features, and confirm whether it is ovarian cancer. Clear cells and chromophobe RCC cells are types of renal cell carcinoma with distinct microscopic appearances: chromophobe RCC cells are pale and larger than clear cells and look different under the microscope. Stage 3A2 cancer has spread to the tissue lining the abdomen and is so small it can only be seen with a microscope. Tumors that appear more different have a higher risk of spreading. IHC is applied to cancer or immune cells and helps identify immunophenotype through chemical marker addition and microscopic analysis.

Cryotherapy, also known as cryosurgery, freezes and destroys precancerous and cancerous cells using a very cold liquid or tool, often liquid nitrogen. It may cause a burning sensation, blister, and scab, which heal over 2 to 3 weeks, and can lead to skin darkening or lightening during healing. Healing from cryotherapy or other treatments continues for 6 to 10 weeks and involves skin darkening and lightening. Skin grafts, which are patches of skin removed from one body area and transplanted to another, may be performed during or after procedures like PDEMA/Mohs or standard surgical excision, either the same day or a few days later, and are used to help heal wounds or reduce scarring. Skin grafts or flapping may be needed for other wounds, and scar treatment and aftercare are recommended for skin around wounds. An oncology team, which treats many cases of rare anal cancer, is essential for effective healing.

Normal human cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes, totaling 46 chromosomes. These chromosomes are tightly packaged structures composed of DNA molecules and other molecules, containing most of the genetic information in the cell. Each chromosome holds thousands of genes, which are coded instructions for the proteins cells produce. Most genes provide information about a specific protein. A mutation is a change in the genetic code. A gene located on chromosome 9 at position 9p3 produces the p16 protein. DNA is tightly packaged into chromosomes, and genes are fundamental units of heredity that direct protein synthesis.

Bladder cancer surgery and bladder removal surgery are associated with common side effects including bleeding, blood clots, kidney problems, infection, sexual dysfunction, incontinence, and urinary diversion problems. Blood clots can occur in the legs or lungs, causing leg swelling, chest pain, and shortness of breath, and are prevented in patients post-surgery with blood thinners. Other treatment options include reduced or shorter courses of BCG therapy, eliminating BCG maintenance, systemic therapy, clinical trials, or intravesical chemotherapy, especially when BCG is not available. Patients at highest risk of cancer recurrence are prioritized for treatment. High-grade gliomas, though unrelated to bladder conditions, are linked to blood clots and develop rapidly, causing symptoms. A biopsy is required to confirm ovarian cancer, which is unrelated to bladder cancer.

Survivorship addresses physical, emotional, and financial issues faced by cancer survivors, including managing long-term side effects, staying connected with a primary care doctor, and adopting a healthy lifestyle. Sexual dysfunction, such as decreased desire to have sex, may result from treatment or cancer and is caused by lack of energy, self-consciousness after surgery, stress, or depression. Urinary incontinence may also occur but can be improved with pelvic floor exercises. Treatment options for bladder cancer depend on the stage, grade, patient’s overall health, and preferences, with transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) used to examine and remove bladder tumors and radical cystectomy being the most common surgery for muscle-invasive cases. The oncologist develops a survivorship care plan that includes treatment history, short- and long-term side effects, cancer return monitoring, care transfer to primary care, and recommendations for health and well-being. Patients should discuss treatment options, preferences, and concerns with their care team and make their wishes known. Clinical social workers address mental, behavioral, and emotional issues.

Lynch syndrome is an inherited cancer syndrome caused by mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes, increasing the risk of colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, and urinary tract cancers. It is diagnosed through genetic testing using a blood or saliva sample, analyzed by a pathologist for gene mutations. Individuals with Lynch syndrome or those with cancers showing the dMMR/MSI-H biomarker are recommended for testing. The condition is linked to a family history of colorectal, endometrial, or ovarian cancer, and patients should disclose personal or family history of these cancers to their provider. While most colon and rectal cancers occur for unknown reasons, inherited mutations in MMR genes are a known risk factor. Lynch syndrome is distinct from familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), which causes hundreds to thousands of benign polyps in the colon and rectum that can become invasive cancer, typically by age 50 in classic FAP.

The book is organized into chapters covering testing, treatment, CML phases, and various health assessments, including fertility, performance status, and genetic testing. It provides screening recommendations for individuals assigned female at birth and discusses testing options for pregnant, lactating, and symptomatic individuals, including breast pain, nipple discharge, skin changes, and lumps. Each chapter ends with a "Questions to Ask" section to help patients understand available information and make informed decisions about care. The book addresses concerns about fertility, pregnancy, and treatment effects, noting that treatment may affect fertility and that patients should consider consulting a fertility specialist. It also covers supportive care as part of cancer care and explains treatment options based on cancer subtype, age, risk factors, and potential outcomes such as cure, long-term control, effectiveness, time, cost, quality of life, and life extension. Being diagnosed with a brain tumor, such as primary CNS lymphoma, is described as frightening and overwhelming, and the book aims to help patients navigate treatment decisions.

A complete blood count (CBC) and comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) are standard blood tests used in the evaluation of AML, with CBC including differential, uric acid, LDH, B12, and folic acid. These tests, along with medical history and physical exam, assess past and current health, including illnesses, injuries, infections, family history, and symptoms. A medical history records all health issues, treatments, and medications, including over-the-counter drugs and herbal supplements such as St. John’s wort, turmeric, and green tea extract, which may interact with prescribed therapies. Additional required tests include blood clotting studies, bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with genetic and biomarker analysis, HLA typing, brain imaging (CT or MRI as indicated), and FDG-PET/CT if extramedullary leukemia is suspected. Some tests, like LDH, immunoglobulins, and CT scans, are useful but not required. Patients must report all supplements to their care team, as they can affect treatment efficacy. DNA sequencing may identify mutations in TP53 and IGHV genes.

Classic follicular lymphoma (FL), classified under ICC as grade 1 or 2, is treated as such and is characterized by centroblasts correlating with tumor grade, which determines treatment. Grade 3A FL may be treated as classic FL or DLBCL depending on the center and cell types; grade 3B FL, known as follicular large B-cell lymphoma, is treated as DLBCL. Almost everyone with FL has a chromosome translocation or excess BCL2 protein. Transformed FL can progress to DLBCL before, during, or after treatment. NLPHL is marked by popcorn-shaped cells, typically grows slowly, but can transform into DLBCL in rare cases. The patient guide covers CLL, includes tests, watch and wait, treatments, Richter transformation, and supportive care, and advises reading Chapter 5 on Richter transformation. It does not discuss glassy-cell carcinomas, sarcomas, or other tumor types. DLBCL commonly affects lymph nodes, spleen, liver, bone marrow, and other tissues.

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is an aggressive type of lung cancer that forms from cells lining the inner airways of the lungs and appears small and blue under a microscope. It is the second most common lung cancer, accounting for about 1 in every 10 lung cancers, and is much less common than non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). SCLC grows rapidly and is often detected when symptoms appear or when routine blood tests show abnormalities; it is less frequently found on x-rays or CT scans. Smoking is the main cause, with almost all people with SCLC having smoked or currently smoking, often more than a pack a day. SCLC can cause symptoms by preventing the lungs from receiving air and may lead to paraneoplastic syndromes. It is divided into small cell carcinoma and combined (small and non-small) cell lung carcinoma, the latter of which is usually treated like SCLC. SCLC is classified as a type of lung cancer and is distinct from non-urothelial bladder cancers, which include squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and small cell carcinoma. Information about SCLC and NSCLC is available through NCCN.org/patientguidelines and the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app.

Ink marks on the skin help position the body accurately for daily radiation treatments by aiding in consistent positioning during therapy. The radiation oncologist devises a treatment plan that aims radiation beams at the anal tumor and lymph nodes in the pelvis and groin. The patient lies on a table in the same position as during simulation and may use devices to prevent movement, which helps target the tumor. A technician operates the machine from a nearby room, can see, hear, and speak with the patient at all times, and is available for hearing and talking. The patient does not see, hear, or feel the radiation and may hear noises during treatment. Each session lasts less than 10 minutes. Devices and ink marks are used to ensure precise targeting, and the patient remains alone in the treatment room.

After thyroid surgery, pathologic examination determines cancer type and risk. If the tumor is benign, no further treatment is needed, but lifelong levothyroxine is required for hormone replacement. If follicular or oncocytic cancer is confirmed, further treatment depends on surgical results; a concerning amount of cancer remaining may lead to another surgery, RAI therapy, radiation therapy, systemic therapy, or monitoring. Invasive cancer requires removal of the rest of the thyroid, often via completion thyroidectomy. After any treatment, levothyroxine is typically started to maintain low or normal TSH levels. For low-risk or minimally invasive cases, monitoring may be chosen instead of surgery. Hormone replacement is not always needed after lobectomy due to continued thyroid hormone production. Levothyroxine may be prescribed on a case-by-case basis to maintain normal TSH levels, especially in benign nodules or for watch-and-wait approaches. Biomarker testing may guide targeted or immunotherapy eligibility.

T2 stage indicates a tumor size between 2 and 4 cm in head and neck cancers, or a tumor of 2 cm or less with depth of invasion exceeding 5 mm. It describes tumor growth into the parapharyngeal space and nearby soft tissues, including the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles and prevertebral muscles. In spinal tumors, T2 means the tumor is confined to three adjacent vertebrae. T4b denotes very advanced local disease with tumor invasion of the lateral pterygoid muscle, pterygoid plates, lateral nasopharynx, skull base, or masticator space, and encasement of the internal carotid artery. T4a indicates moderately advanced disease with invasion of the larynx, extrinsic tongue muscle, medial pterygoid, hard palate, or mandible. Soft tissues include medial and lateral pterygoids and prevertebral muscles. Tumor size is measured in centimeters, with a golf ball equivalent to 4 cm and a baseball to 7 cm.

The prostate gland, located deep in the pelvis just below the bladder and between the hip bones, is about the size of a ping-pong ball and is a key part of the male reproductive system. Prostate cancer occurs when cells in the prostate gland grow out of control due to genetic mutations, leading to uncontrolled cell multiplication and crowding out of normal cells. Age is the biggest risk factor, with risk increasing as you age; everyone with a prostate is at risk, and Black people and those with certain inherited genetic mutations are at greater risk. Most cases grow slowly and remain within the prostate, known as early-stage or localized prostate cancer, which has not spread beyond the gland. Advanced-stage cancer has spread to other parts of the body through metastasis. Not everyone diagnosed with prostate cancer requires treatment.

A bone tumor is an abnormal growth of cells in bone and may be cancerous or noncancerous, commonly occurring in the metaphysis, especially near growth plates. The metaphysis lies between the physis (growth plate) and diaphysis, and the physis is composed of cartilage that eventually leaves a physeal scar after skeletal maturity. Giant cell tumor of bone (GCTB) is typically not cancerous but requires aggressive treatment to prevent bone damage; it arises in the metaphysis and extends into the epiphysis, which is covered with cartilage to form a joint. Osteosarcoma also starts in the metaphysis, near growth plates. Chapter 8 discusses GCTB treatment options and explains that infant acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) treatment differs from that of other age groups, with infants defined as those under 12 months of age.

Endocrine therapy blocks estrogen receptor signaling and is used to treat breast cancer by preventing hormones from binding to receptors. Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) like tamoxifen block estrogen from attaching to receptors, while selective estrogen receptor degraders (SERDs) like fulvestrant block and destroy receptors. Aromatase inhibitors, including exemestane (steroidal) and non-steroidal agents like anastrozole and letrozole, inhibit estrogen production by blocking the aromatase enzyme without affecting ovarian estrogen. mTOR, a cell protein that promotes cell growth, can become overactive and reduce endocrine therapy effectiveness; everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, is used in combination with exemestane, fulvestrant, or tamoxifen to restore therapy effectiveness. For ER-low–positive invasive breast cancer—defined as 1 to 10 estrogen receptors per 100 cancer cells—endocrine therapy may not be recommended. Endocrine therapy also includes testosterone-suppressing therapy for males assigned male at birth.

Chemotherapy regimens for anal cancer, including mitomycin and capecitabine, mitomycin and 5-FU, and 5-FU and cisplatin, are recommended for stages I, II, and III and are used in combination with radiation therapy, administered five days per week. Intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) is the preferred radiation technique. For stage II anal cancer in complete remission, surveillance includes annual imaging for three years. If a patient achieves complete remission after platinum-based chemotherapy and cancer returns more than six months later, it is classified as platinum-sensitive, indicating platinum-based chemotherapy is effective. Alternative regimens include paclitaxel and carboplatin, or paclitaxel, carboplatin, bevacizumab, and maintenance bevacizumab. Radiation therapy may be used if no prior radiation was given, especially for cancer returning to inguinal lymph nodes, with chemotherapy potentially given in addition. Follow-up and surveillance is recommended and located on page 22.

A hematologist is an expert in blood diseases and blood cancers and treats these conditions, while a medical oncologist treats cancer in adults using systemic drug therapy and often coordinates care with the team. The care team may include a hematologist, medical oncologist, and pathologist, who analyzes biopsy samples to provide cancer diagnosis, staging, and biomarker testing information. Team members, including the medical oncologist, should understand how the patient feels, what they need, what is working and what is not, and their treatment goals. Patients are encouraged to share their insights about their bodies and experiences to help the team understand their needs and preferences. A list of team members’ names and contact information should be maintained to support communication. The patient’s input is vital in evaluating what is working and what is not in their treatment.

G1 is well differentiated and classified as low grade, indicating slow growth and a low risk of recurrence. G2 is moderately differentiated and classified as intermediate grade, with some sources labeling it as high grade. G3 is poorly differentiated and classified as high grade, indicating rapid growth and spread, with cancer cells looking very different from normal cells; it is the highest grade for breast cancers. GX indicates the grade cannot be determined. High grade (G3) corresponds to fast growth, while low grade (G1) corresponds to slow growth. Local excision is only recommended for low-grade (G1) and intermediate-grade (G2) perianal cancers. Grade measures cancer aggressiveness, with G1, G2, and G3 representing increasing levels of differentiation and aggressiveness.

Lynch syndrome, caused by inherited mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes, is the most common hereditary cause of colon and uterine cancers and can also lead to ovarian cancer, which typically starts at a younger age when associated with Lynch syndrome or BRCA mutations. It is linked to dMMR/MSI-H tumors, which trigger testing for Lynch syndrome. Lynch syndrome accounts for a small portion of kidney tumor cases. Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is another rare inherited cancer syndrome that also accounts for a small portion of kidney tumor cases. Other inherited syndromes, including Beckwith-Wiedemann, Carney complex, PGL/PCC, Li-Fraumeni, MEN 1, MEN 2, NF1, and VHL, each account for a small portion of kidney tumor cases and are rarer than Lynch syndrome or FAP. All rectal cancer cases require tumor testing for MMR gene mutations.

Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a blood cancer that occurs only if a person has the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph) or the BCR::ABL1 gene. The Philadelphia chromosome is a abnormal chromosome 22 formed by a fusion of parts from chromosomes 9 and 22, and it is the hallmark of CML. The BCR::ABL1 gene, not present in normal blood cells and not inherited from parents, produces a new protein that causes uncontrolled blood cell growth, leading to CML. This uncontrolled growth results in excessive white blood cells, particularly granulocytes, and sometimes abnormal platelet levels. Treatment for CML focuses on stopping the activity of the BCR::ABL1 protein. Patients should receive care at medical centers experienced in CML and advocate for the best care.

The HPV vaccine available in the United States protects against 9 strains of HPV, including the highest-risk strains, and is now recommended for adults aged 45 and under, though it was previously advised only for adolescents and young adults. It works best in younger people, ideally under age 13, because they are less likely to have been exposed to HPV. The vaccine can prevent new HPV infections but does not treat existing infections or HPV-related cancers. Two other HPV vaccines are available in other parts of the world: one protects against HPV-16 and HPV-18, and another protects against HPV-16, HPV-18, and two additional types. Vaccination is most effective when administered before exposure to HPV, and it helps prevent HPV infection.

A radiation oncologist prescribes and plans radiation therapy to treat cancer, delivering it as part of a multidisciplinary care team. The assessment team includes a thoracic radiologist, who specializes in chest imaging using CT or X-ray to detect cancer spread to the lungs, and an interventional radiologist. The team also includes a pulmonologist, expert in lung diseases, and a thoracic surgeon, expert in chest operations. Other members include a medical oncologist and a radiation oncologist. Chest imaging helps determine if cancer has spread to the lungs, and the care team, including these specialists, collaborates with the patient to develop a personalized treatment plan. The team may also include a diagnostic radiologist, pathologist, gastroenterologist, surgical oncologist, geriatrician, registered dietitian, genetic counselor, and palliative care provider.

Pembrolizumab (Keytruda) and nivolumab (Opdivo) are PD-1 inhibitors used as checkpoint inhibitors to treat dMMR/MSI-H cancers and tumors with high tumor mutational burden (TMB-H), PD-L1 positivity, or MSI-H/dMMR biomarkers. Pembrolizumab is preferred for dMMR/MSI-H cancers, TMB-H tumors, and PD-L1-positive cancers, and is used in combination with chemotherapy (e.g., cisplatin and paclitaxel) or as monotherapy. It is also used in squamous cell skin cancer and other cancers. Nivolumab is used in dMMR/MSI-H cancers before colectomy and for TMB-H tumors. Cemiplimab (Libtayo) is another PD-1 inhibitor used for squamous cell skin cancer and other cancers, especially when biomarkers are absent. Chemotherapy is recommended for pMMR/MSS cancers and some stage 2 pMMR/MSS cancers after colectomy, while no chemotherapy is recommended for stage 1 or stage 2A/2B dMMR/MSI-H cancers post-colectomy. Radiation therapy may be used alongside systemic therapy for unresectable cancers. Bevacizumab is a targeted therapy used with chemotherapy in metastatic cervical cancer. Systemic therapy, including immunotherapy, is first-line for advanced or lymph node-positive cancers.

Anal cancer is rare and stigmatized, making it difficult for survivors to find peer support and leading to hesitation in sharing diagnoses due to fear of judgment, which can result in isolation and distress. Treatment, including radiation therapy, often affects bowel and bladder function, sexual health, and causes fatigue, dyspnea, and insomnia, contributing to a lower quality of life. Survivors commonly experience anxiety, depression, and difficulty coping, and are encouraged to seek mental health resources. Social workers play a key role by helping patients access mental health and financial support, navigate insurance and financial stresses, and cope with everyday problems. Treatment teams are expected to proactively address mental health concerns; if not, patients should speak up. Survivors are encouraged to get a mentor and, upon recovery, mentor others. The NCCN Guidelines for Patients provide information on distress during cancer care, and care for colorectal cancer begins with self-care.

Phase 1 trials study the dose, safety, and side effects of an investigational drug or treatment approach and look for early signs of effectiveness or helpfulness. Phase 2 trials evaluate how well the drug or approach works against a specific type of cancer. Phase 3 trials test the drug or approach against a standard treatment; if results are favorable, the drug may be approved by the FDA. Phase 4 trials study the long-term safety and benefit of an FDA-approved treatment. These phases collectively assess safety, efficacy, and long-term outcomes in cancer treatment.

Radiation is a type of X-ray used in small doses to create images of the inside of the body and may be referred to as a radiograph. Chest X-rays can detect cancer spread to the lungs, are used to monitor treatment results, and use small amounts of radiation; they are fast and painless. Diagnostic CT scans, similar to X-rays, provide clearer images of body tissues and use more radiation than regular CT scans, often with a contrast agent that highlights tissues for the scanner. MRI does not use radiation and is safe for most people, helping determine cancer depth in the rectal wall and spread to lymph nodes. Adjuvant therapy, given after primary treatment, reduces cancer recurrence risk and may include radiation to eliminate residual cancer cells or prevent recurrence in high-risk patients. Treatment for anal cancer involves a team of digestive health experts with experience in chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, and imaging. Everyone with anal cancer is encouraged to consider enrolling in a clinical trial. Tumor markers, found in body tissue or fluid, may indicate cancer presence.

Nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) and oropharyngeal cancer are types of throat cancer that share similar symptoms with less serious conditions, often leading to delayed diagnosis until an advanced stage. NPC should not be confused with laryngeal or esophageal cancer. HPV testing by p16 is recommended for throat cancer and is used to gain more information about the cancer, as p16 is also found in cervical, vulvar, melanoma, and esophageal cancers. A biopsy of the tumor is performed, and tissue may be taken from the throat, lymph node, or other body sites. Information on all these cancers—including mouth, throat, and nasopharyngeal cancer—is available through NCCN.org/patientguidelines and the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app.

The epidermis consists of three main cell types: squamous cells, basal cells, and melanocytes. Squamous cells are thin, flat cells found in the upper part of the epidermis, resembling fish scales and forming the skin's surface; they are also found in the lining of the nasopharynx, anal canal, and digestive tract, where cancers like nasopharyngeal cancer and anal cancer often originate in squamous cell carcinoma. Basal cells are located in the lower part of the epidermis, in the basal cell layer, where they constantly divide to form new cells that move upward, become flatter, and eventually turn into squamous cells, replacing them. Melanocytes, located in the lower epidermis and top layer of skin, produce melanin, which determines hair, skin, and eye color and protects the skin from harmful ultraviolet rays. Most skin cancers arise in the epidermis, primarily in squamous or basal cells.

Family health history includes information about diseases such as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, focusing on the age at diagnosis, cause of death, and age of death among relatives. It reflects patterns of health conditions in family members and is gathered from close blood relatives including parents, siblings, half-siblings, grandparents, aunts and uncles, nieces and nephews, and grandchildren. Parents and siblings are primary sources of information, with grandparents being first- and second-degree relatives of parents. Relatives diagnosed with cancer are asked about the type, age at diagnosis, and whether they died from it.
