A family history of certain diseases increases the risk of conditions like CLL, with relatives being 7 to 8 times more likely to develop it if there is a family history. Ancestry, including countries of origin, is also recorded. This information is shared with a health care provider and may lead to genetic counseling or testing if a germline mutation is suspected. Geneticists study how traits are passed through genes from parents to children and provide diagnosis, treatment, and counseling for genetic disorders.

A lung nodule is a small mass of tissue in the lungs, often found by chance during a medical examination. Many people have lung nodules, which are mostly not cancer but some may be. Lung nodules can result from cancer, infections, scar tissue, or other health conditions. When detected by imaging, nodules may receive additional scans to evaluate for cancer. If a nodule is unlikely to be cancer, patients may be referred for lung cancer screening. Lung nodule experts assess whether a nodule is cancerous. Most lung nodules are not cancer, though some are. Small masses of tissue are found in the lungs and are commonly referred to as lung nodules.

Early-stage prostate cancer is localized, meaning it is contained entirely within the prostate and has not spread beyond it. It grows slowly and remains within the prostate, and is classified as highly treatable and often curable. The earlier it is diagnosed and treated, the greater the likelihood of living without cancer for the rest of one's life. Imaging tests may be used to check for spread but are often not needed. Patients may not require immediate treatment, and their care team evaluates the risk of cancer worsening using key characteristics. This condition is distinct from advanced-stage prostate cancer, which involves cancer cells spreading outside the prostate (metastasis). Information about early-stage prostate cancer is available through the NCCN Guideline for Patients.

The digestive system takes in food, breaks it down, absorbs nutrients, and removes waste. Food moves from the mouth through the esophagus to the stomach, where stomach contractions, along with enzymes and acid, break it down into chyme. Chyme enters the small intestine, where nutrients are absorbed into the bloodstream. The system includes the esophagus, stomach, liver, pancreas, small intestine, colon, rectum, and anus. Enzymes and acid in the stomach facilitate food breakdown, while the small intestine is key to nutrient absorption. Waste is removed from the body via the digestive tract. Blood, though not part of the digestive system, transports oxygen and nutrients throughout the body and removes waste, supporting the immune system and preventing bleeding.

Infertility is defined as the inability to produce children and can result from damage to sperm or eggs, particularly due to chemotherapy or radiation therapy, which damages the hormone-making function of ovaries and testicles. Fertility preservation options include sperm banking (semen cryopreservation), egg freezing (oocyte cryopreservation), and ovarian tissue banking, which involves removing and freezing ovarian tissue containing eggs for later reimplantation. Ovarian transposition is a surgical procedure that moves ovaries and fallopian tubes out of the radiation beam’s range to protect them. Patients of childbearing age who plan to have children should inform their doctor or care team, who will discuss fertility-related risks and may refer them for counseling. These methods enable having children after cancer treatment by preserving reproductive cells or tissues.

Testosterone is the main androgen produced by the testicles and plays a key role in prostate cancer growth. Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) deprives cancer of androgens, leading to tumor shrinkage or slowed growth. Castation, a drastic reduction of testosterone, is used to treat prostate cancer and can be achieved through hormone-lowering medication or surgical removal of the testicles (orchiectomy). Orchiectomy is classified as hormone therapy because it removes the primary source of testosterone and is permanent and irreversible, unlike drug-based hormone therapy, which can be reversed upon medication stoppage. Androgens, including testosterone, are male hormones that activate cells and are carried by the blood. Hormones bind to receptors on cells, including breast cancer cells, where they may cause cancer to grow. Endocrine therapy uses hormones like ethinyl estradiol, fluoxymesterone, and megestrol acetate (Megace ES) to treat breast cancer, though it is not known how these hormones stop cancer growth. Symptoms may appear when the body produces too much of a hormone.

The procedure involves removing a visible tumor using a scalpel, followed by excision of a thin layer of surrounding tissue, with the surgical margin evaluated under a microscope. If cancer cells are detected, additional tissue is removed until no cancer cells remain at the edges. Standard surgical excision, performed in a medical office with local numbing, removes the tumor and surrounding tissue, with a surgical margin of at least 1 cm free of cancer cells indicating no further treatment is needed; less than 1 cm or presence of cancer cells requires further treatment such as re-excision or radiation therapy. Curettage and electrodesiccation, also performed in a medical office with local numbing, scrapes off the tumor using a thin tool and cauterizes the base with an electric needle to kill remaining cancer cells and stop bleeding, potentially repeated up to three times. Wounds may heal without stitches or through secondary intention healing, requiring up to six weeks of dressings, with healing time depending on size, depth, and area.

A colectomy is a surgery to remove the cancerous part of the colon, with the healthy ends of the colon attached together, and can be performed using either an open method involving a large abdominal cut or a minimally invasive method involving few small cuts and insertion of tools to see and remove tissue. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) testing, also known as a liquid biopsy, analyzes a blood sample to detect small pieces of DNA released by tumor cells, including microscopic disease that may remain after colectomy. This test can detect microscopic rectal cancer cells and may help predict whether cancer is likely to return or other outcomes, but ctDNA testing is currently being studied in clinical trials and is only recommended as part of a clinical trial. The test is not a standard treatment but a research-based approach to monitor cancer recurrence risk.

Changes in AML cells include deletion, insertion, inversion, amplification, translocation, and point mutation, all of which are detected by mutation testing and are unique to AML cells. Ewing sarcoma is characterized by a gene fusion between the EWS gene on chromosome 22 and a member of the ETS gene family (FLI1, ERG, ETV1, ETV4, FEV), with FLI1 being the most common; this fusion results from a translocation between chromosomes 11 and 22 (t(11;22)), which is common in Ewing sarcoma. The tumor originates in the bone marrow and commonly occurs in the diaphysis of long bones or flat bones such as the pelvis or scapula. Translocation involves the switching of parts between two chromosomes, leading to gene fusion, and is a key genetic abnormality in both AML and Ewing sarcoma.

Patients should ask questions and take notes during appointments, and may ask a friend or family member to assist. Caregivers should also ask questions. Medical documents such as insurance forms, medical records, and test results should be organized, and a contact list should be maintained, including details about the specific type of cancer, treatment, and dates, and updated with the primary care physician. Patients should set up a MyChart or health record account to track appointments and communicate with the care team, though portal messages are not immediately seen by nurses or physicians. Urgent concerns should be addressed by calling the triage phone number. Patients should be prepared to list any illness or injury and when it occurred. The care team should be consulted to learn how best to communicate, especially in emergencies. A patient had a consultation with a CLL specialist, who answered all questions thoroughly and provided satisfactory advice. Patients should bring a companion to doctor visits and not fear asking their care team questions.

Local excision is a surgical treatment option for some early-stage, low-risk perianal cancers, particularly stage I and IIA cancers, involving removal of the tumor and a small area of surrounding tissue. It may be used instead of chemoradiation for slow-growing stage I and II cancers. However, local excision is not appropriate if the tumor has invaded the sphincter muscle or the muscle layer (a T2 tumor), as this indicates high-risk features. Testing of removed tissues may reveal high-risk features or muscle invasion, both of which necessitate additional treatment. If such features are found, the preferred next step is transabdominal surgery. Cancer grade is also a key factor in determining eligibility for local excision.

Depression and anxiety are common in patients with primary brain tumors, affecting 1 in 3 and up to 3 out of 4, respectively, and leading to psychological distress. Patients may experience depression, anxiety, and sleep issues, and their treatment team screens for distress as part of cancer care. Psychologists and psychiatrists, classified as mental health experts, help manage depression, anxiety, and other mental health conditions that affect how a person thinks and feels or emotional well-being. Anxiety following a cancer diagnosis may be managed by a social worker, who is available in some cancer centers. Patients are encouraged to inform their treatment team of stress or overwhelm and to ask for help, as coping alone is not recommended. The care team can also be consulted about access to clinical trials. Radiation therapists deliver radiotherapy treatments.

T1 stage anal cancer refers to a tumor size of 2 cm or smaller that has not spread to nearby lymph nodes or distant areas from the anus, and is described as T1, N0, M0. In this stage, the tumor has a depth of invasion of 5 mm or less. If surgery confirms the cancer is T1 and the tumor is low risk, no further treatment is needed, and surveillance begins. T1 stage in other contexts, such as spinal tumors, means the tumor is confined to one or two adjacent vertebrae or is 8 cm or smaller. In cervical cancer, T1 is not directly defined but is associated with tumor size and depth. Stage 1B3 cervical cancer (larger than 4 cm, confined to cervix) and stage 2A2 cervical cancer (larger than 4 cm, extending into upper vagina) share similar characteristics and may be treated as early-stage or locally advanced, with chemoradiation preferred over early-stage treatment.

A scope, a long thin tube with a light and camera lens, is used to examine the body, including the back of the throat, larynx, and oropharynx, and can be inserted through the mouth or nose. It has a light and camera lens to send images to a television or computer monitor, helping guide a doctor during procedures like biopsies. Endoscopes are commonly used for head and cancer cases, aiding in determining tumor size and spread and taking tumor samples. Fiberoptic nasopharyngolaryngoscopy examines the larynx and nearby structures, performed while the patient is awake with a topical spray for comfort. Laryngoscopy, using a laryngoscope with a fiberoptic light, examines the back of the throat, including the larynx and hypopharynx. Numbing medicine is applied to the throat or nose before procedures to reduce discomfort. Tonsils, located at the back of the throat, are masses of lymph tissue that help trap germs entering through the nose or mouth.

A neurological exam assesses alertness, balance, coordination, reflexes, hearing, and senses, including touch and smell, and may include an eye exam to evaluate the health of nerves in the back of the eyes. This exam is a key step in diagnosing primary CNS lymphoma, which is distinguished from lymphoma in other body parts or different diseases and confirmed through neurological exam, imaging (MRI or CT scan), and biopsy. Biopsy involves taking tissue or fluid samples to look for cancer. The parietal lobe is responsible for intelligence, language, reading, sensation, and sensory perception. Treatment for primary CNS lymphoma includes chemotherapy, radiation therapy, stem cell transplant, or a combination of these, with participation in a clinical trial of a new therapy also recommended.

Depression screening is required for all patients, and tobacco and alcohol use histories are collected as known risk factors for head and neck cancer, with both potentially limiting treatment effectiveness and affecting survival. Patients are advised to quit smoking and limit alcohol use during treatment and are encouraged to speak to their care team. A complete head and neck exam, mirror and fiberoptic exam if needed, and medical history are part of the initial evaluation. Biopsies of the primary tumor may be performed with HPV testing via p16, and imaging including chest CT (with or without contrast), CT/MRI of the primary tumor and neck, and FDG-PET/CT may be conducted. Dental exams include Panorex x-ray or CT without contrast. Additional evaluations include nutrition, speech, swallowing, and hearing tests. Fertility counseling and hepatitis B screening are provided if diagnosed. Head and neck cancer surgery is complex and influenced by tobacco, alcohol use, tumor location, and other health conditions.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) begins in the bone marrow and is diagnosed through the removal and testing of bone marrow samples before treatment starts. These samples are reviewed by a pathologist who specializes in diagnosing AML. Treatment for AML is divided into phases and aims to achieve remission, with a treatment plan developed jointly by the patient and their care team based on blood tests, bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, and imaging studies. Patients should speak to their care team about their feelings, side effects, and insurance coverage for tests, and regularly discuss treatment goals and next steps. Side effects, which can vary in number and severity and depend on the type, length, and dose of treatment, typically appear soon after treatment begins and often resolve after treatment ends, though some may be long-term and appear years later. Managing side effects is a shared effort between the patient and care team, with patients encouraged to speak up about symptoms like nausea and vomiting and ask about management options.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment that uses high-energy beams from electrons, photons, or protons to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. Electrons are used to treat superficial tumors, while photons are used to treat deeper and more invasive tumors. Photons, which include high-energy x-rays, are particularly effective for deeper tumors and more invasive cancers. Protons are also used in radiation therapy but are not specifically linked to tumor depth in the provided passages. External beam radiation therapy (EBRT) commonly uses electrons and photons. Radiation therapy also helps treat pain caused by cancer.

Radioactive material and dyes are injected into the breast tumor area to identify sentinel lymph nodes, which may contain cancer cells. The dyes travel through lymphatics to reach lymph nodes, where they are detected by a surgeon. Sentinel nodes are removed and tested by a pathologist; if cancer is present, additional lymph nodes may be removed. Radioactive material enters instruments placed in the body during treatment, such as in brachytherapy, which is administered over a couple of days with all treatments completed within 1 to 2 days. Instruments are placed and left in the body until all treatments are given, and patients must remain in bed until treatment is complete to prevent instrument movement. Chemicals in dyes and other products are linked to an increased risk of bladder cancer, and treatment varies depending on the phase of the cancer.

LHRH agonists, such as goserelin (Zoladex), leuprolide (Lupron), and triptorelin, reduce testosterone by causing testicles to stop producing it and are used in androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) for prostate cancer. LHRH agonist anti-androgens, including nilutamide, flutamide, and bicalutamide, block cancer cells from using testosterone and are part of long-standing hormone therapies for prostate cancer. LHRH antagonists, such as degarelix and relugolix (Orgovyx), also reduce testosterone and are used in ADT; relugolix is available as a tablet taken once daily. Most LHRH agonists and antagonists are administered via injection, typically monthly or every 2 to 4 months. Surgical castration is as effective as ADT. Some chemotherapy drugs are taken orally as tablets or capsules, but this is distinct from hormone therapies.

A primary care provider or physician provides prevention and treatment, including full skin exams that occur at least once a year, with patients required to engage in prevention between exams. These providers help manage other health conditions, especially those affected by cancer treatment, and may be the first to suspect lung cancer. Prevention is a key component of care, and removing polyps can prevent cancer before it starts. Both primary care providers and physicians deliver prevention services, ensuring comprehensive health management.

Foods high in insoluble fiber and fiber supplements, such as psyllium-based products like Metamucil, can help manage bowel problems by slowing and thickening stool, reducing frequency, urgency, and fecal incontinence. Over-the-counter anti-diarrheal medicine thickens watery stool and helps with frequent bowel movements. Scar tissue can impair anal muscle function, leading to changes in bowel habits including fecal incontinence, increased bowel movements, gas, and fecal urgency. The thyroid uses iodine, which is obtained from the diet and found in certain foods and iodized salt, to produce hormones. If cancer cannot be removed surgically, does not take up iodine, and is progressing, treatment may include radiation therapy or targeted therapy. Nutritionists and dietitians provide guidance on suitable foods and diets for specific medical conditions.

Medical records, test results, and insurance forms are stored in a medical binder, which is organized to include sections for questions and notes. Patients can view medical records and test results through online patient portals, which allow access to both records and test results. These records can be downloaded or printed and added to the binder. The binder is brought to appointments as it may be needed at any time. Patients are advised to ask many questions during appointments and to bring a family member to take notes.

Estrogen and progesterone are hormones that play key roles in breast development and the menstrual cycle, respectively. Hormone receptor (HR) testing on biopsy samples determines if a new tumor is hormone receptor-positive, with most breast cancers being so. Estrogen receptor (ER) is stimulated by estrogen and promotes cancer cell survival and proliferation; blocking estrogen or ER signaling can halt tumor growth. Endocrine therapy blocks estrogen and progesterone to treat hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. Estrogen is primarily produced by the ovaries and fat tissue, while progesterone is mainly produced by the ovaries. Luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH), also known as gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), is produced by the hypothalamus and stimulates ovarian estrogen and progesterone production. Test results, including blood tests, imaging, and biopsy findings, determine treatment. FES, a radioactive form of estrogen, may replace FDG PET-CT in estrogen receptor-positive cancers. Menstrual periods indicate premenopause, and treatment may cause amenorrhea, which can return in individuals under 35.

To get the best care, patients should advocate for themselves and their child, ask questions, and make shared decisions with the care team. They must understand what test results mean, including those from biopsy and imaging studies, which inform the treatment plan. Patients should keep copies of test results, particularly blood tests, imaging results, and reports about their specific cancer. Online patient portals provide convenient access to these results and should be used to review them. It is essential to discuss results with a healthcare provider. Seeking the opinion of an ALL specialist and treatment at an experienced pediatric leukemia center increases the likelihood of receiving desired care. The NCCN Guidelines for Patients can help understand cancer care.

Stage 3A bladder cancer is limited to fatty tissue surrounding the bladder or a single nearby lymph node and may invade reproductive organs, without spreading to lymph nodes or organs far from the bladder. Stage 3B has the same traits as Stage 3A but has spread to multiple pelvic lymph nodes and has not spread to lymph nodes or organs far from the bladder. Stage 3C has visible cancer on the abdominal lining, larger than 2 cm, may involve lymph nodes in the back of the abdomen, and may have spread to the outer surface of the liver or spleen. Stage 4 bladder cancer has grown through the bladder wall and may spread to lymph nodes or organs far from the bladder. Stage 4A involves invasion of the pelvis or abdominal wall, cancer cells in fluid around the lungs (malignant pleural effusion), and spread to distant lymph nodes. Stage 4B involves spread to the inside of the liver or spleen, distant lymph nodes, or other organs like bones, lungs, or distant sites, and is classified as metastatic bladder cancer. Chemotherapy is used to kill cancer cells and may be given before or after surgery. Imaging (CT, MRI, PET/CT) assesses response to systemic therapy in Stage 4B or distant recurrences.

Systemic therapy, including chemotherapy, kills both cancer cells and healthy cells, leading to damage that causes side effects such as hair loss, cracked skin, mouth sores, nausea, and vomiting. These side effects depend on the drugs used, the dose, and the individual patient. Chemotherapy harms healthy cells, which may result in potentially harsh side effects. Targeted therapy drugs attack specific parts of cancer cells to kill them or slow their growth and spread, and are used in primary CNS lymphoma, often combined with chemotherapy. Because targeted therapy primarily targets cancer cells, it may have fewer side effects than chemotherapy. Patients and their care teams share responsibility for managing side effects, and patients should speak up about bothersome effects like nausea and vomiting and ask about options for managing treatment effects. Supportive care information is available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app.

Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is caused by a specific abnormal gene, BCR::ABL1, formed when a piece of chromosome 9 breaks off and trades places with a piece of chromosome 22. This exchange results in a fused gene, BCR::ABL1, and a shortened chromosome 22 known as the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome. The Ph chromosome is the hallmark of CML and is present in all cases of the disease. BCR::ABL1 is the primary driver of CML and is responsible for the development of Philadelphia chromosome chronic myeloid leukemia. Without the Ph chromosome or the BCR::ABL1 gene, CML does not develop. The break and exchange between chromosome 9 and chromosome 22 is the defining genetic event in CML.

Adrenal glands, small yellow glands located on top of each kidney and part of the endocrine system, produce hormones including cortisol, aldosterone, and DHEA, which regulate metabolism, blood pressure, and body features. Adrenal tumors form in one or both adrenal glands and are mostly benign; adrenal cancer, a rare cancer originating in the adrenal glands, is uncommon. Most adrenal tumors have no known cause, though hereditary conditions—mutations passed down through genes—can increase risk, accounting for only a small portion of cases. These tumors are not typically fast-growing and appear dim on FDG-PET scans, which use 18-fluorodeoxyglucose to detect active cancer cells that use sugar more rapidly. FDG-PET can help assess if neuroendocrine tumors are becoming more aggressive. Androgens, produced by adrenal glands, testicles, and ovaries, contribute to body features like hair growth and body shape.

Pelvic lymph nodes, the closest to the cervix, are commonly the first site where cervical cancer spreads and are tested during pre-treatment surgical staging. Para-aortic lymph nodes, located in the abdomen, may also be removed and tested, especially in stage 3C cervical cancer or when cancer has spread beyond the cervix. Sentinel lymph node biopsy uses a radioactive substance or special dye injected near the cervix to identify and remove sentinel nodes for cancer detection. These nodes are visible with a special camera and tested for cancer to determine the extent of disease. Removing lymph nodes helps limit cancer cell spread and guides treatment decisions. Radical hysterectomy, recommended for stage 1A2, 1B1, 1B2, and 2A1 cancers, includes pelvic lymph node evaluation and may involve para-aortic lymph node removal. Pre-treatment surgical staging involves removing and testing both pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes to inform treatment planning. Fertility-sparing surgery is rarely used for stage 1B2 cancers, with abdominal surgery generally preferred.

Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), a highly specialized type of external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), delivers high-dose radiation to small areas over 3 to 5 treatments and is used to treat metastatic cervical cancer and limited numbers of small metastases in stage IV anal cancer that metastasized before diagnosis and was never treated with radiation. SBRT is typically applied to tumors in the liver, lungs, or bone and requires only a few treatment sessions. Radiation therapy, including SBRT, may be used to relieve pain and bothersome side effects from distant tumors. Metastatic cervical cancer is very hard to cure, and SBRT is a viable option for treating metastatic cervical cancer. SBRT is also an option for stage IV anal cancer with limited small metastases.

Breast cancer begins in the cells of the breast, most commonly as a carcinoma originating in epithelial cells that line the inner or outer surfaces of the body. These epithelial cells are located within the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs) of the breast and are the primary site for most breast carcinomas. The most common types are ductal or lobular. Cancer arises from these epithelial cells and may spread into surrounding tissue; invasive breast cancer has grown outside the ducts or lobules and can disseminate through lymph or blood to lymph nodes or other parts of the body.

Tumor markers, such as carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), CA 15-3, and CA, can be detected in blood or biopsy tissue; an increase in their levels may suggest cancer progression, though they are not reliable for detecting breast cancer. Imaging tests assess cancer spread beyond the prostate, showing cancer size and location. Removal of tumor tissue and nearby lymph nodes is part of pathologic staging and provides a more accurate picture of cancer spread than imaging, helping determine treatment options. Pathologic staging, based on surgical staging, gives the most accurate assessment of cancer spread and guides post-surgery treatment. A follow-up examination 8 to 12 weeks after treatment may detect cancer progression, requiring a biopsy for confirmation.

Imaging scans, including computed tomography (CT) and MRI, are used to detect cancer and assess its presence in suspicious lesions, bone, nerves, and deep soft tissue. A CT scan uses an x-ray machine to create detailed pictures of body areas, which can show the number, location, and size of lymph nodes. Depth of invasion (DOI) measures how deep a tumor has grown into tissue layers, not tumor thickness, and can be calculated using imaging scans like MRI. A DOI greater than 4 cm or invasion of structures such as the cortical bone of the mandible, maxilla, maxillary sinus, or skin of the face indicates advanced local disease (T4a). As DOI increases, the risk of regional lymph node metastases also increases. If biopsy confirms cancer has spread to lymph nodes, a CT scan of those nodes is recommended to evaluate their extent. Tumors may grow through the oral mucosa, and DOI reflects the depth of this invasion.

The esophagus is a 10-inch-long, 1-inch-wide muscular tube that transports food from the throat to the stomach, primarily through peristalsis during swallowing, which is aided by gravity and pressure. It is normally empty except during swallowing and has two sphincters—one at the top and one at the bottom—that remain closed otherwise. The esophagus wall consists of four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria, and tunica adventitia. Thin, flat cells in the inner lining of the esophagus can develop into esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Early-stage esophageal cancer is confined to the esophagus with a small tumor not involving any lymph nodes. The esophagus is part of the digestive tract and connects the mouth to the stomach. A procedure under anesthesia in an operating room allows a doctor to examine the esophagus for abnormal growths.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a fast-growing blood cancer that starts in the stem cells of the bone marrow, where abnormal changes prevent myeloid blasts or myeloblasts from maturing into healthy blood cells. This blockage causes a buildup of immature blasts in the bone marrow and blood, leading to insufficient red blood cells, platelets, and white blood cells. The lack of these healthy cells causes serious health issues and makes AML fatal if left untreated. AML is characterized by too many immature white blood cells and is distinct from myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), which involves abnormal blood cells and insufficient healthy cell production but can progress to AML. In MDS, the bone marrow fails to produce enough healthy blood cells and contains abnormal cells in the blood and/or bone marrow.

RAI therapy is recommended for differentiated thyroid cancers at higher risk of recurrence, particularly when cancer has spread beyond the thyroid, invaded blood vessels, or shows high Tg levels post-surgery, large or more than five lymph node involvements, or is a high-grade carcinoma. It is administered orally in liquid or pill form, requiring a low-iodine diet for 1 to 2 weeks and a high TSH level, often achieved by stopping thyroid hormone replacement or using Thyrogen to stimulate TSH and maintain hormone replacement and imaging. Side effects include neck pain, swelling near the jaw, nausea, dry mouth or eyes, and changes in taste or smell. The dose is adjusted for children and patients on dialysis. RAI therapy is used after total thyroidectomy for iodine-uptake cancers and for remnant ablation post-surgery. It is not effective for medullary or anaplastic thyroid cancer. Local therapies, including ablation using probes or electrodes placed directly into or near tumors, treat specific areas and are followed by systemic therapy when needed. Surgery is preferred for recurrent neck cancers, though not always required. Radiation exits the body via urine and body fluids.

The stomach consists of the cardia, fundus, body, antrum, and pylorus. The cardia is the opening where the esophagus connects to the stomach and is a part of the stomach. The fundus is the upper part of the stomach, forming a bulge higher than the cardia, and stores undigested food and gases. The antrum is the lower portion of the stomach where food mixes with enzymes and acid. The esophagogastric junction (EGJ), also known as the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ), is located just below the diaphragm and marks the point where the esophagus joins the stomach; it separates esophageal and gastric contents and contains acid. Tumors originating in the cardia that extend into the esophagogastric junction are classified as esophageal cancers.

Self must be their own advocate by talking to someone who has experienced the same situation, asking many questions—including those they are afraid to ask—to protect themselves, make the best decisions, and receive the best care for their unique circumstances. This involves staying calm, taking care of mental and emotional well-being, getting organized, and being prepared. Patients are advised to ask hard questions and play an active role in their care, as they have an important role in ensuring their own treatment decisions align with their needs. Advocating for self ensures optimal outcomes and active participation in care.

Smoking tobacco is the biggest risk factor for lung cancer, with risk increasing with the number of times and length of time a person smokes; second-hand smoke, consisting of exhaled smoke and smoke from combustible tobacco products, also increases lung cancer risk. People with small cell lung cancer (SCLC) often have a history of smoking more than one pack per day, though some develop SCLC without a smoking history. Risk is higher in individuals over 70, those with prior chest radiation, and those exposed to cancer-causing chemicals like radon and asbestos. Researchers are investigating why some smokers never develop lung cancer and why some non-smokers do. Smoking and heavy alcohol use negatively affect treatment outcomes and increase treatment toxicity, and patients are advised to seek help to quit smoking or vaping through healthcare providers who offer counseling and medications. Quitting smoking reduces the likelihood of new lung tumors. Symptoms may reduce food intake and nutrient consumption, impacting surgery and treatment outcomes. Researchers are also studying ways to prevent smoking-related lung cancer and working on hundreds of clinical trials for glioma treatments.

Grade indicates the abnormality of tumor cells under a microscope and correlates with growth and spread rate. In gliomas, grades 1 and 2 are low-grade: grade 1 tumors grow slowly, are usually benign, and are more common in children, often treatable with surgery; grade 2 tumors have somewhat abnormal cells, grow slowly, may invade tissue, and can recur to become higher-grade. Grades 3 and 4 are high-grade: grade 3 tumors have cells that look unlike normal cells, grow rapidly, and invade nearby tissue; grade 4 tumors have very abnormal cells, grow and spread quickly, and include glioblastoma. In follicular lymphoma (FL), grade is determined by cell composition in germinal centers: centrocytes (smaller, less dividing) and centroblasts (larger, more dividing) form follicles; grade 3B contains only centroblasts, while other grades contain mixtures of both. Higher-grade cancers grow and spread faster than lower-grade ones.

A pelvic exam uses a speculum to view the vagina and cervix and may involve removing cells for a Pap test, which detects cervical cancer or pre-cancer but not ovarian cancer. The exam may also include a rectovaginal exam to check for cancer in the space between the rectum and vagina. An endometrial biopsy of the uterine lining may be performed during the pelvic exam to rule out uterine cancer. The CA-125 test measures a protein in the blood that may indicate ovarian or other cancers but cannot diagnose ovarian cancer alone, as conditions like endometriosis or diverticulitis can raise CA-125 levels, and some ovarian cancers do not elevate it. CA-125 testing is performed before each chemotherapy cycle to monitor treatment response and side effects, alongside imaging and blood tests. A physical exam, including pelvic and rectovaginal exams, is scheduled every 1 to 3 cycles during chemotherapy.

Quality of life refers to a person’s overall enjoyment of life, including their sense of well-being and ability to participate in usual activities, and should be the main priority guiding treatment and care. Successful treatment involves reducing cancer, minimizing cognitive problems, reducing pain, lowering anxiety and stress, carrying out regular activities, being with friends and family, and enjoying life as best as possible. Symptoms such as peeing frequently, difficulty urinating or defecating, and sexual problems are assessed by the doctor or care team to determine their impact on quality of life. Patients are encouraged to answer questions honestly and completely to ensure accurate assessment. Every treatment for primary CNS lymphoma can cause side effects, which are unhealthy or unpleasant physical or emotional conditions. Side effects are tracked for duration and their effect on quality of life, and the effectiveness of treatments used to manage them is evaluated.

Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a stage 0 or noninvasive cancer characterized by cancerous cells that are confined within the ducts of the breast and remain in situ, having not spread to surrounding breast tissue, lymph nodes, or distant sites. These cells are located in the cells that line the ducts and are classified as preinvasive, meaning they have not invaded beyond the ductal lining. DCIS is rated as Tis, with no spread to lymph nodes (N0) or distant sites (M0). It is considered noninvasive and is treated to prevent progression to invasive breast cancer, a more advanced form of the disease. DCIS is a preinvasive condition where cancerous cells are present in situ but have not spread outside the ducts.

A mammogram is an x-ray image of the breast created by pressing the breast between two plates while the patient stands in different positions. Multiple x-rays are taken and combined by a computer to produce detailed pictures of the breast, which may be 2-dimensional (2D) digital or 3-dimensional (3D) tomosynthesis. Screening mammograms are performed regularly when there are no signs or symptoms of breast cancer, while diagnostic mammograms are used for individuals with symptoms such as lumps, pain, nipple discharge, or changes in breast shape, or to examine an abnormal area found in a screening mammogram. Diagnostic mammograms focus on specific areas not clearly seen on screening exams, detect tumors, and determine tumor size. They may include extra compression, magnification views, or rolling the breast. A radiologist evaluates the mammogram and can arrange additional testing immediately if needed. Results from diagnostic mammograms take a few days. Both types use low-dose x-rays and may be used for bilateral imaging. Mammograms are used to plan treatment. Diagnostic mammograms may not be used if a patient has a serious allergy or if their kidneys are not functioning well.

Online patient portals allow patients to access test results, including blood test results and biopsy findings, which are used to determine treatment plans. These results are important for understanding what tests mean and should be discussed with a doctor or health care team to ensure accurate interpretation. Patients are encouraged to ask questions about their test results and use portals to access them, but are advised to wait to discuss results with their health care provider. Portals may also contain communications between health care team members and other information that may require explanation. Full understanding of test results is essential for patients, and direct discussion with a health care provider is recommended before making decisions based on the results.

Interstitial brachytherapy is a specialized treatment technique used for advanced cervical cancer involving the parametrium, where thin hollow tubes or catheters are placed either in the tumor or in tissues adjacent to the tumor. This method relies on catheters and thin hollow tubes to deliver radiation directly to the cancer site. Interstitial brachytherapy is best performed at cancer centers with experience in this technique and in treating advanced cervical cancer. Cancer centers also have experience in managing mediastinal gray zone lymphoma (MGZL), which is distinct from primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma (PMBL), and patients with MGZL are best managed in such centers. Many cancer centers offer integrative oncology programs.

A higher PSA level can result from a larger prostate, which is measured via transrectal ultrasound or MRI scan, and is adjusted for size using PSA density—calculated by dividing PSA level by prostate size. A PSA density above 15 ng/mL² indicates a greater likelihood of prostate cancer, especially in men with small or very small prostates who may have cancer despite low PSA levels. PSA levels above 5 ng/mL are suspicious in men in their 40s, 5 ng/mL or higher in those in their 60s, and 10 ng/mL or higher at any age is a danger sign. PSA levels may rise after ejaculation or vigorous exercise, so doctors may advise avoiding sex and exercise for 2 or 3 days before testing to allow levels to return to baseline. PSA alone does not provide a complete picture; imaging tests like PET scans, which highlight potentially cancerous cells or irregular, hardened prostate tissue, are used alongside PSA to improve prostate health assessment.

Oxaliplatin, a platinum-based chemotherapy drug used in rectal cancer treatment, can cause nerve damage (neuropathy) affecting the fingers and toes, manifesting as numbness, tingling, cramping, or pain. This nerve damage is a common side effect of oxaliplatin-containing regimens and is more pronounced in intraperitoneal chemotherapy, which also causes more severe side effects than intravenous chemotherapy, including infections, kidney damage, and pain in the belly. Other drugs like irinotecan cause abdominal cramping, nausea, diarrhea, and hair loss. Platinum-based drugs such as carboplatin and cisplatin can damage kidneys; cisplatin is contraindicated in those with poor kidney function and may cause hearing problems. Nerve damage and sensory disturbances like numbness and tingling are also associated with gliomas, typically occurring on one side of the body. Patients should consult their treatment or care team for a complete list of side effects and report any medications or supplements that may interact with chemotherapy. Side effects can be prevented or alleviated with appropriate interventions.

Intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) is an advanced type of external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) that uses many small beams of different intensities to deliver a high dose of radiation to the tumor while minimizing exposure to surrounding normal tissue. IMRT is used to treat cervical and anal cancer and is the preferred and recommended method for anal cancer. It reduces radiation to critical nearby structures such as the bowel, bladder, external genitalia, and hip joints, which helps lower treatment-related side effects. The technique employs small beams with varying strengths to precisely target the tumor and limit radiation to normal tissue, making it effective in preserving nearby organs and reducing complications. IMRT is a type of external radiation therapy that allows for precise dose delivery and is distinct from brachytherapy, which delivers radiation directly to the tumor.

A skin punch biopsy removes a small piece of skin and connective tissue using a hand-held tool, and stitches are often used to close the skin opening. This procedure is performed when a predisposition condition to leukemia is suspected, as the DNA obtained from skin tissue has not been altered by acute myeloid leukemia (AML), allowing analysis for inherited genes that increase leukemia risk. Inherited genes, which can be passed from a biological parent to a child, are linked to hereditary cancer syndromes and may contribute to a family history of leukemia, influencing treatment decisions. While blood tests at diagnosis can reveal genetic changes in leukemia, these may not reflect the genetic changes present at birth. Therefore, skin punch biopsy helps assess inherited genetic predisposition, distinguishing between acquired and inherited factors in leukemia development.

Mediastinal gray zone lymphoma (MGZL) and non-mediastinal gray zone lymphomas are the two main types of gray zone lymphomas. MGZL occurs in individuals aged 20 to 40, assigned male at birth, and is characterized by a large mediastinal mass; it may involve lymph nodes above the collar bone (supraclavicular). Non-mediastinal gray zone lymphomas occur in older persons, have a higher rate of bone marrow involvement, include extranodal disease, and are more advanced in stage than MGZL. Lymph nodes above the collar bone may be involved in MGZL. An expert hematopathologist review is essential to confirm the diagnosis of MGZL, which is distinct from and treated differently from primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma.

HER2 is found on all cells; high amounts cause cell growth and division. Some breast cancers have too many HER2 genes or receptors, making them HER2-positive, also called HER2 overexpression or amplification. HER2 testing includes immunohistochemistry (IHC) and in situ hybridization (ISH). IHC measures HER2 receptors, estrogen, and progesterone receptors; an IHC score of 3+ indicates HER2-positive, 0 or 1 indicates HER2-negative, and 2 requires further testing. ISH counts HER2 gene copies and is used when IHC is unclear. HER2 testing should be performed on all new tumors using a tumor biopsy. HR-negative (HR-) breast cancers lack both estrogen and progesterone receptors and are sometimes called hormone-negative; these cancers grow faster than others and require both estrogen and progesterone receptors to be negative for classification. Breast cancer has estrogen receptors in about 1 out of every 100 cancer cells.

Cancer grade measures how aggressive the cancer is and reflects how fast it is expected to grow and spread, based on how abnormal cancer cells look under a microscope. A pathologist determines the grade by comparing cancer cells to normal cells; the more different the cells appear, the higher the grade. Higher grades correlate with faster growth and spread, and a higher score means the cancer is likely to grow and spread quickly. This is distinct from cancer stage, which describes how far the cancer has spread from its origin. Tumor tissue is removed via biopsy, either before or after surgery, and tested to determine both cancer type and grade. High-grade cancers grow and spread more rapidly than low-grade ones. The grade helps guide treatment decisions, including the choice of therapy, monitoring, or intervention, and is influenced by factors such as age, overall health, and gender.

First-line therapy for metastatic anal cancer involves platinum-based chemotherapy, including regimens such as carboplatin and paclitaxel, FOLFOX, FOLFCIS, modified DCF, or 5-FU and cisplatin. Carboplatin and paclitaxel is preferred over 5-FU and cisplatin based on research. Chemotherapy, a systemic therapy that affects the whole body, is most commonly given intravenously via infusion through a tube into a vein, typically in the arm, and can also be administered orally. Patients should ask their treatment team about frequency, duration, and delivery method. The presence of the PD-L1 biomarker influences first-line regimen selection, with bevacizumab possibly added to preferred regimens for PD-L1-positive cancers. Chemotherapy is also an option for cancer returning to lymph nodes in the groin. Systemic therapy, including chemotherapy and immunotherapy, is used for bladder cancer.

Enrollment in a clinical trial is free and has no fee for participants. The study sponsor covers research-related costs, including the study drug. Participants may incur indirect costs such as transportation or child care due to extra appointments. Participants continue to receive standard cancer care, which is billed to and often covered by insurance, but they are responsible for copays and any uncovered costs for this care. Indirect costs are associated with additional appointments and may include transportation and childcare. The study sponsor pays for research-related costs, which include the study drug.

Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) uses a thin needle to extract small tissue or fluid samples from suspicious areas, including thyroid nodules and lymph nodes, and is recommended when a biopsy is needed. It is performed when other biopsies are not safe and may be guided by ultrasound. Core biopsy (CB) removes larger tissue samples using a needle, sometimes with suction (vacuum-assisted core biopsy), and is used to assess abnormal lymph nodes. Incisional biopsy removes a part of a lymph node through a cut, while excisional biopsy removes the entire abnormal area and is not preferred but may be necessary if other methods fail or are not feasible. These procedures do not impair the body’s ability to fight infections. Abnormal lymph nodes, which may become enlarged as cancer progresses, are evaluated for cancer cells using imaging and FNA or core biopsy; if cancer cells are found, the node is classified as node positive. Bone marrow biopsies and aspirations, performed together on the back of the hip bone, remove core samples and liquid cells but are not usually required for diagnosis.

The areola is a ring of darker breast skin that contains the nipple, which is a raised tip within the areola. The nipple-areola complex (NAC) refers to both the nipple and the areola, and it includes both structures. Small tubes called ducts connect milk-producing lobules to the nipple, carrying breast milk. Lobules appear as tiny clusters of grapes. Ducts connect lobules and the nipple, and the NAC is also described as referring to the nipple, the areola, or both. The areola is defined as darker breast skin, and the nipple is located within it.

HER2-targeted therapy treats HER2-positive breast cancer and is most often combined with chemotherapy, though it may also be used alone or with endocrine therapy; examples include trastuzumab (Herceptin), pertuzumab, and T-DM1. CDK4/6 inhibitors, such as abemaciclib (Verzenio), palbociclib (Ibrance), and ribociclib (Kisqali), are used in hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer when combined with endocrine therapy to prolong cancer control and are distinct from HER2-targeted therapies. Premenopausal patients on CDK4/6 inhibitors must receive ovarian suppression. Ovarian suppression is achieved using LHRH agonists, which stop LHRH production and thereby halt ovarian hormone release. These inhibitors are part of a broader class including mTOR and PARP inhibitors, with specific agents like everolimus and olaparib. Trastuzumab has substitutes including kanjinti, ogivri, and ontruzant.

Carcinoma in situ (CIS), designated as Tis or Stage 0, is a flat, aggressive patch of cancer cells confined to the surface of the bladder lining, specifically within the squamous cell layer, and has not grown beyond its starting point. It is classified as non-muscle-invasive and is considered serious due to its fast growth. Stage 0 includes two subgroups: Stage 0a, where cancer cells grow from the inner lining toward the bladder's hollow center without penetrating the wall, and Stage 0, which stands for CIS. CIS is also referred to as an intraductal tumor. In bladder cancer, T0 indicates the tumor cannot be found, while muscle-invasive cancer (stages 2, 3, and 4) has penetrated the bladder muscle and requires more intense treatment. Stage 1 involves cancer growing through the inner lining into connective tissue.

Stage 1A ovarian cancer is confined to one ovary with an intact outer sac (capsule), no cancer on the outer surface of the ovary, and no cancer cells in ascites or washings. Stage 1B involves cancer in both ovaries, with intact capsules, no cancer on the outer surface, and no cancer cells in ascites or washings. Both stages have no evidence of spread beyond the ovaries and no cancer cells in ascites or washings. The FIGO system defines ovarian cancer stage based on tumor extent, lymph node involvement, and distant spread, with early-stage cancers having better outcomes than advanced ones. Stage 1C includes cancer in one or both ovaries with surgical spill, cancer on the outer surface, or cancer cells in ascites or washings. Advanced cancers tend to have worse outcomes, and other factors like general health are important for prognosis.

Early-stage cervical cancer is often treated with surgery, which may involve removing only a portion of the cervix or, more commonly, the entire cervix, typically through an abdominal incision (laparotomy). Minimally invasive laparoscopic surgery, involving a few small abdominal cuts, is an alternative that results in less pain, less scarring, and a shorter recovery time, and may be used in select cases such as when cancer is limited to the ovaries. Laparoscopy should only be performed by a gynecologic oncologist experienced in the procedure. A gynecologic oncologist, an expert in surgery and chemotherapy for gynecologic cancers, should perform the initial surgery and is a key member of the treatment team, which also includes a medical oncologist and a radiation oncologist. Surgery is a primary treatment option, with other treatments including radiation therapy, chemoradiation, brachytherapy, systemic therapy, and clinical trials depending on cancer extent.

Staging cancer involves assessing the extent of the tumor (T), including its size and growth into nearby areas; the spread to nearby lymph nodes (N), which determines the number and location of affected nodes; and spread to distant sites (M), indicating metastasis to organs like lungs or liver. The grade of cancer (G) describes how closely cancer cells resemble normal cells, with well-differentiated (G1) cells looking normal. Staging systems like the AJCC and TNM combine these factors to assign a final numbered stage, with anatomic staging based on tumor size, lymph node status, and distant metastasis, and prognostic staging including tumor grade. Biomarker testing checks for genes, proteins (e.g., p16, estrogen, progesterone, HER2), or mutations to guide treatment. Not all staging details are available at initial evaluation; additional information may be gathered during treatment. Doctors may explain staging differently than described. Imaging helps determine tumor extent and size, which guides treatment decisions. Patients who do not remember or understand their stage should ask for more information.

Small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) is the same cancer as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), with identical cancer cells. The distinction lies in cell location: CLL is primarily found in the blood and bone marrow, while SLL is mostly in lymph nodes and the spleen. If blood tests show fewer than 5,000 cancerous cells, the condition is classified as SLL; if more than 5,000, it is classified as CLL. Treatment for both is the same, and recommendations for CLL are considered applicable to SLL. The disease is often referred to as CLL/SLL. Lymph nodes and the spleen play a key role in fighting infections and may become swollen due to the buildup of CLL or SLL cells. A biopsy of lymph nodes or bone marrow is performed when blood test results are unclear to confirm a diagnosis of SLL. Lymph node tests can confirm the presence of small lymphocytic lymphoma.

Simulation is the first step in radiation therapy, requiring the patient to lie on their back, stay very still, and may involve a prop to maintain position. A CT scan is performed during simulation to obtain images of the cancer sites, which are used by the radiation team and radiation oncologist to create a personalized treatment plan using computer software. The treatment plan specifies the radiation dose and number of sessions, is tailored to the patient’s body and cancer, and considers prior pelvic radiation. If intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) is used, the patient lies in a frog-legged position during both simulation and treatment. Simulation is followed by several days for planning, dose calculation, and quality assurance before treatment sessions begin. Treatment sessions begin after simulation and involve the patient lying on a table in the same position. The practice recommends chemotherapy regimens matching NCCN guidelines, offers IMRT, and provides measures to minimize side effects, which may be short-term or permanent. The practice treats anal cancer as a primary condition and other conditions, has experience in treatment, and can offer a shorter radiation course.
